# Brazilian Culture: full content

Everything in the guide at https://brazilianculture.biblioverse.org/ as plain Markdown, stop by stop, with a link to each page. Content updated November 2026.

## Famous Brazilians

https://brazilianculture.biblioverse.org/famous-brazilians.html


### Famous worldwide

- **Pelé**: (Sport) The King of Football. The only player to win three World Cups (1958, 1962 and 1970), he turned the number 10 shirt into a legend. Died in 2022.
- **Marta**: (Sport) Six-time FIFA World Player of the Year and the top scorer in World Cup history, men or women, with 17 goals.
- **Ayrton Senna**: (Sport) Three-time Formula 1 world champion (1988, 1990 and 1991). He died at Imola in 1994 and the whole country stopped for his funeral. He is still a hero to people who never saw him race.
- **Ronaldo**: (Sport) World champion in 1994 and 2002, when he scored both goals in the final. Twice FIFA’s best player in the world, he came back from injuries that would have ended any other career.
- **Ronaldinho**: (Sport) The smile and the dribbling of Barcelona. A World Cup winner in 2002 and Ballon d’Or in 2005, he even got a standing ovation from Real Madrid fans at the Bernabéu.
- **Neymar**: (Sport) Brazil’s all-time top scorer and the most followed Brazilian on Instagram. Santos, Barcelona, PSG and back to Santos.
- **Vinícius Júnior**: (Sport) Real Madrid forward, named FIFA’s best player in the world in 2024. He has also become a global voice against racism in football.
- **Maria Esther Bueno**: (Sport) Winner of 19 Grand Slam titles, including three Wimbledon singles crowns. She ruled world tennis in the 1950s and 60s and the centre court at the Rio Games bears her name.
- **Guga Kuerten**: (Sport) Three-time Roland Garros champion and world number one in 2000. He drew a heart in the Paris clay and won over all of France.
- **Rebeca Andrade**: (Sport) Brazil’s most decorated Olympian, with six medals, and Olympic champion on vault (2020) and floor (2024). She grew up in Guarulhos and went on to beat Simone Biles.
- **Gabriel Medina**: (Sport) Brazil’s first world surfing champion, with three titles (2014, 2018 and 2021). He led the generation known as the “Brazilian Storm”.
- **Anderson Silva**: (Sport) “The Spider”: the longest title reign in UFC middleweight history, with strikes that looked like special effects.
- **Amanda Nunes**: (Sport) “The Lioness”, from Bahia, widely seen as the greatest female MMA fighter ever, and a UFC champion in two weight classes at once.
- **Rayssa Leal**: (Sport) “The Little Fairy”: she went viral at seven skateboarding in a fairy costume and won Olympic silver in Tokyo at 13. Bronze followed in Paris.
- **Fernanda Montenegro**: (Film and TV) The grande dame of Brazilian acting. The first Latin American nominated for the Best Actress Oscar, for Central Station (1998), she was still working past 90.
- **Fernanda Torres**: (Film and TV) Golden Globe winner for Best Actress in a Drama and Oscar nominee for I’m Still Here, 26 years after her mother, Fernanda Montenegro. At home she is also a comedy idol.
- **Wagner Moura**: (Film and TV) Captain Nascimento in Elite Squad and Pablo Escobar in Narcos. In 2026 he won a Golden Globe for The Secret Agent and became the first Brazilian nominated for the Best Actor Oscar.
- **Sônia Braga**: (Film and TV) From Gabriela and Dona Flor to Kiss of the Spider Woman and Aquarius. Brazil’s biggest star in Hollywood since the 1980s.
- **Rodrigo Santoro**: (Film and TV) Xerxes in 300, Paulo in Lost and Hector in Westworld. One of the Brazilians with the most international credits.
- **Alice Braga**: (Film and TV) Sônia Braga’s niece, she went from City of God to I Am Legend and the series Queen of the South.
- **Carmen Miranda**: (Film and TV) The “Brazilian Bombshell”, with fruit on her turban, was the highest-paid woman in the United States in 1945 and shaped the world’s image of Brazil.
- **Gisele Bündchen**: (Fashion) The girl from Horizontina, in southern Brazil, who ended the heroin-chic era and was for years the world’s highest-paid model.
- **Adriana Lima**: (Fashion) Born in Salvador, she was a Victoria’s Secret Angel for almost two decades, the longest run in the brand’s history.
- **Alessandra Ambrosio**: (Fashion) From Erechim, in the far south. Another long-serving Angel and one of the best-known Brazilian models abroad.
- **Machado de Assis**: (Literature and ideas) The grandson of freed slaves, he founded the Brazilian Academy of Letters and wrote Dom Casmurro and The Posthumous Memoirs of Brás Cubas. One of the great 19th-century novelists in any language.
- **Clarice Lispector**: (Literature and ideas) Born in Ukraine and raised in Recife. The Hour of the Star and The Passion According to G.H. made her a cult author worldwide.
- **Jorge Amado**: (Literature and ideas) He took Bahia to the world with Gabriela, Clove and Cinnamon and Captains of the Sands, translated into dozens of languages.
- **Guimarães Rosa**: (Literature and ideas) A doctor and diplomat who reinvented Portuguese in The Devil to Pay in the Backlands (1956), an epic of the Brazilian interior.
- **Carolina Maria de Jesus**: (Literature and ideas) A waste-paper collector who wrote about hunger in notebooks found in the rubbish. Child of the Dark (1960) was translated into more than a dozen languages.
- **Paulo Coelho**: (Literature and ideas) The Alchemist (1988) is one of the best-selling books in history. He wrote songs with rock star Raul Seixas before becoming Brazil’s most-read author in the world.
- **Oscar Niemeyer**: (Art and design) He designed Brasília and Pampulha and worked on the UN headquarters team. His concrete curves gave modernism a Brazilian accent. He worked until he died, aged 104.
- **Tarsila do Amaral**: (Art and design) She painted Abaporu (1928), Brazil’s most famous painting and the spark for the Cannibalist Manifesto: swallow what comes from abroad and give it back Brazilian.
- **Roberto Burle Marx**: (Art and design) The landscape designer behind the wave pavement at Copacabana and Flamengo Park. He brought native plants into the modern garden.
- **Sebastião Salgado**: (Art and design) The photographer from Minas Gerais behind Genesis and Workers, some of the most powerful portraits of humanity ever made. Died in 2025.
- **Luva de Pedreiro**: (Creators) Iran Ferreira, from Bahia, who kicked a ball around dirt pitches shouting “receba!” (“take that!”). He went viral around the world in 2022 and later even filmed with Cristiano Ronaldo’s son.
- **Casimiro**: (Creators) A streamer from Rio, known as “Cazé”, who reacts to everything with humour. His channel CazéTV broadcast the World Cup and Olympics on YouTube and broke audience records.
- **Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva**: (Politics) From migrant child and factory worker to president, re-elected in 2026, he is the Brazilian politician best known around the world. Obama once called him “the man”.
- **Anitta**: (Music) Brazil’s biggest pop star. She came from Honório Gurgel, in Rio, and in 2022 became the first Brazilian to top Spotify’s global chart, with Envolver.
- **Marcelo**: (Sport) Real Madrid’s left-back for 15 years, with five Champions League titles, a huge smile and even bigger curls.
- **Bruna Marquezine**: (Film and TV) A telenovela star since childhood, she reached Hollywood in DC’s Blue Beetle (2023).
- **Hugo Calderano**: (Sport) The greatest table tennis player the Americas have produced. In 2025 he became the first player from the Americas to win the sport’s World Cup, beating Chinese stars in Macau, and was runner-up at the World Championships in Doha, the best run ever by a South American.
- **Torben Grael**: (Sport) A sailor with five Olympic medals, two of them gold, and the skipper who won the 2008–09 Volvo Ocean Race, the round-the-world yacht race.
- **Isaquias Queiroz**: (Sport) The canoeist from Bahia with five Olympic medals, including gold in Tokyo. As a child he survived a fall that cost him a kidney.

### Famous in Brazil

- **Silvio Santos**: (TV) From street vendor to owner of the SBT network. “The Boss” hosted Sundays for over 60 years, throwing paper planes made of cash into the audience. Died in 2024.
- **Chacrinha**: (TV) The “Old Warrior”: a horn, a costume and salt cod thrown into the crowd. He coined the saying “if you don’t communicate, you’re in trouble”.
- **Hebe Camargo**: (TV) The “queen of TV”, known for her sofa, her jewels and her little kisses for guests. A pioneer of Brazil’s first broadcasts in 1950.
- **Xuxa**: (TV) The “Queen of the Little Ones”. Xou da Xuxa shaped generations of children and also succeeded across Latin America and in the US.
- **Faustão**: (TV) “Ô loco, meu!” He hosted Domingão do Faustão on Globo for more than 30 years.
- **Gugu Liberato**: (TV) Domingo Legal, the Gugu bathtub and the endless Sunday ratings war against Faustão. Died in 2019.
- **Ana Maria Braga**: (TV) The morning show Mais Você, its recipes and Louro José, a puppet parrot who became a national character.
- **Jô Soares**: (TV) A comedian on Viva o Gordo and a novelist, he was for years the country’s last interview before bed on Programa do Jô. Died in 2022.
- **Pedro Bial**: (TV) A foreign correspondent who became the face of Big Brother Brasil and its elimination speeches. Now hosts Conversa com Bial.
- **Luciano Huck**: (TV) Two decades of Caldeirão do Huck and, since 2021, Sundays on Domingão. A regular subject of political speculation.
- **Fátima Bernardes**: (TV) The face of the Jornal Nacional news for 14 years, she then hosted the morning show Encontro on Globo.
- **Glória Pires**: (Acting) A child star who shone in Vale Tudo and Mulheres de Areia, playing the twins Ruth and Raquel. She became a meme for saying “I’m not able to give an opinion” while commentating the Oscars.
- **Regina Duarte**: (Acting) The eternal “little sweetheart of Brazil”, lead of Malu Mulher and Roque Santeiro.
- **Ruth de Souza**: (Acting) A pioneer of the Black Experimental Theatre, she was the first Brazilian nominated for an acting prize at an international festival, for Sinhá Moça (Venice, 1954).
- **Marília Pêra**: (Acting) From Pixote to Brega & Chique, one of the most versatile actresses in Brazilian film, TV and theatre. Died in 2015.
- **Lima Duarte**: (Acting) Sinhozinho Malta in Roque Santeiro. More than 70 years in the business, since the first days of Brazilian TV.
- **Taís Araújo**: (Acting) The first Black lead of a Globo telenovela, in Da Cor do Pecado (2004). Xica da Silva (1996) had already been a landmark on the Manchete network.
- **Regina Casé**: (Acting) From the theatre group Asdrúbal Trouxe o Trombone to The Second Mother and the show Esquenta!. The face of popular culture on TV.
- **Garrincha**: (Sport) “The Joy of the People”. Bent legs, impossible dribbles and the 1962 World Cup almost on his own. To many, he was as much of a genius as Pelé.
- **Zico**: (Sport) The “White Pelé”, Flamengo’s greatest idol and the star of the unforgettable 1982 Brazil side that didn’t win the World Cup.
- **Éder Jofre**: (Sport) The “Golden Bantam”, world boxing champion in two divisions and considered one of the greatest bantamweights ever.
- **Hortência and Paula**: (Sport) The duo who led women’s basketball to the 1994 world title and Olympic silver in 1996. Hortência is in the Hall of Fame.
- **Oscar Schmidt**: (Sport) “Holy Hand”, for years the top scorer in basketball history with 49,737 points, and the hero of the 1987 Pan American final against the US. Inducted into the Hall of Fame in 2013, he died in 2026.
- **Giba**: (Sport) The star of volleyball’s golden generation, Olympic champions in Athens (2004) and three-time world champions under coach Bernardinho.
- **Robert Scheidt**: (Sport) A sailor with five Olympic medals, two of them gold, and a long list of world titles.
- **Carlos Drummond de Andrade**: (Culture) The poet of “in the middle of the road there was a stone”. A statue of him sits on a bench in Copacabana, where everyone stops for a photo.
- **Monteiro Lobato**: (Culture) Creator of the Yellow Woodpecker Ranch stories, with Emília and Narizinho. He shaped the childhoods of generations and today his work is also debated for its racism.
- **Mauricio de Sousa**: (Culture) Brazil’s “Walt Disney”, creator of Monica’s Gang. Almost every Brazilian learned to read with these comics.
- **Ariano Suassuna**: (Culture) The writer from Paraíba behind A Dog’s Will, a play that became one of the country’s best-loved works.
- **Ziraldo**: (Culture) The cartoonist behind The Nutty Boy and O Pasquim, a satirical paper that irritated the dictatorship. Died in 2024.
- **Felipe Neto**: (Creators) One of the world’s biggest YouTubers, with tens of millions of subscribers, and a regular voice in Brazilian public debate.
- **Whindersson Nunes**: (Creators) From Piauí, he started with home videos and once had Brazil’s biggest YouTube channel. He also packs theatres with stand-up.
- **Tatá Werneck**: (Creators) The queen of improv, discovered on MTV. She hosts Lady Night on Multishow and is one of the most followed people in the country.
- **Virginia Fonseca**: (Creators) An influencer from Goiânia who shares her daily life with millions and created the cosmetics brand Wepink.
- **Larissa Manoela**: (Acting) A child star on SBT’s Carrossel. In 2023, her dispute with her parents over her own money became a national debate.
- **Maísa**: (Acting) She became a sensation at three years old through hilarious chats with Silvio Santos on TV, and grew up in front of the whole country.
- **Marina Ruy Barbosa**: (Acting) The red-haired Globo telenovela star of Império and Totalmente Demais, and a fixture in fashion.
- **Gusttavo Lima**: (Music) The “Ambassador” of sertanejo, known for Balada (Tchê Tcherere Tchê Tchê). His shows and livestreams draw huge crowds.
- **Wesley Safadão**: (Music) From Ceará, he took electronic forró to the top of the charts with Camarote and plenty of other hits.
- **Simone Mendes**: (Music) One half of the duo Simone & Simaria, she went solo in 2022 and became one of the biggest voices in sertanejo.
- **Mario Sergio Cortella**: (Culture) A philosopher and teacher from Paraná, author of bestsellers such as Por Que Fazemos o Que Fazemos? and one of the country’s best-known public speakers, with many videos online.
- **Paulo Freire**: (Literature and ideas) The educator behind Pedagogy of the Oppressed (1968), one of the most cited works in the social sciences. Official patron of Brazilian education.

## Music

https://brazilianculture.biblioverse.org/music.html


### Artists and bands

- **Tom Jobim**: (Bossa nova and MPB · 1958) Co-writer of The Girl from Ipanema, one of the most recorded songs in the world. He recorded with Frank Sinatra and Rio’s airport is named after him.
- **João Gilberto**: (Bossa nova and MPB · 1958) He invented the bossa nova guitar beat. Chega de Saudade (1958) changed Brazilian music in two minutes.
- **Vinicius de Moraes**: (Bossa nova and MPB · 1958) The “little poet”, a diplomat and the lyricist of The Girl from Ipanema and Chega de Saudade.
- **Elis Regina**: (Bossa nova and MPB · 1965) To many, Brazil’s greatest singer. Elis & Tom (1974) is a classic and O Bêbado e a Equilibrista became the anthem of the political amnesty. Died in 1982.
- **Chico Buarque**: (Bossa nova and MPB · 1966) The songwriter of Construção and Cálice, who dodged the dictatorship’s censors with pseudonyms and metaphors. Also a novelist and winner of the Camões Prize.
- **Caetano Veloso**: (Tropicália · 1967) A leader of Tropicália, jailed and exiled by the dictatorship. Sampa and Alegria, Alegria are part of the national imagination.
- **Gilberto Gil**: (Tropicália · 1967) The Bahian behind Aquele Abraço and Andar com Fé. He was Minister of Culture (2003–2008) and is a member of the Brazilian Academy of Letters.
- **Gal Costa**: (Tropicália · 1967) The voice of Baby and Divino, Maravilhoso and one of the boldest singers of her time. Died in 2022.
- **Os Mutantes**: (Tropicália · 1966) Rita Lee and the Baptista brothers: psychedelic rock that later influenced the likes of Kurt Cobain and Beck.
- **Maria Bethânia**: (Bossa nova and MPB · 1965) The dramatic voice of Bahia and Caetano’s sister. One of the country’s longest-serving and most revered singers.
- **Milton Nascimento**: (Bossa nova and MPB · 1967) The voice “God would sing with”, according to Elis. Clube da Esquina (1972) is among the greatest records ever made in Brazil.
- **Djavan**: (Bossa nova and MPB · 1976) From Alagoas, the writer of Oceano and Flor de Lis, with a way of composing nobody can imitate.
- **Roberto Carlos**: (Pop and romantic · 1959) “The King”. From the Jovem Guarda scene to tens of millions of records sold and a Christmas TV special on Globo for decades.
- **Tim Maia**: (Pop and romantic · 1970) The father of Brazilian soul, of Azul da Cor do Mar and Descobridor dos Sete Mares. As famous for his voice as for the shows he cancelled.
- **Rita Lee**: (Rock · 1966) The “queen of Brazilian rock”: she left Os Mutantes to become the country’s best-selling female rocker. Died in 2023.
- **Raul Seixas**: (Rock · 1973) The “Cheerful Madman”. At any gig in Brazil, someone will still shout “Toca Raul!” (“Play some Raul!”).
- **Legião Urbana**: (Rock · 1982) Renato Russo and the anthems of a generation, from Faroeste Caboclo to Tempo Perdido and Pais e Filhos.
- **Cazuza and Barão Vermelho**: (Rock · 1981) Exagerado, Ideologia, O Tempo Não Para. Cazuza turned his own illness into a public protest. Died in 1990.
- **Os Paralamas do Sucesso**: (Rock · 1982) Rock with ska and horns from Herbert Vianna, Bi Ribeiro and João Barone. Also big in Argentina.
- **Titãs**: (Rock · 1982) Eight voices behind Comida and Bichos Escrotos. “We don’t just want food” became a protest line.
- **Sepultura**: (Rock · 1984) From Belo Horizonte to the world. Roots (1996) blended metal with Brazilian percussion, was recorded with the Xavante people and changed the genre.
- **Cartola**: (Samba · 1928) Founder of the Mangueira samba school and writer of As Rosas Não Falam and O Mundo é um Moinho. He made his first album at 66.
- **Dorival Caymmi**: (Samba · 1938) The Bahian who sang of the sea and its fishermen. He wrote O Que É Que a Baiana Tem?, a hit for Carmen Miranda.
- **Ary Barroso**: (Samba · 1939) Writer of Aquarela do Brasil, known abroad simply as Brazil. It went global through Walt Disney and became a kind of second anthem.
- **Clara Nunes**: (Samba · 1971) The first Brazilian woman to sell over 100,000 records, she brought Afro-Brazilian religions into popular success.
- **Beth Carvalho**: (Samba · 1968) The “Godmother of Samba”, who discovered Fundo de Quintal and took pagode from Rio’s backyards onto the radio.
- **Zeca Pagodinho**: (Samba · 1983) Deixa a Vida me Levar (“Let life carry me”): the Rio rascal whose song became a national philosophy.
- **Luiz Gonzaga**: (Northeast and sertanejo · 1941) The “King of Baião”, with an accordion and a leather hat. Asa Branca is practically the anthem of the backlands.
- **Chitãozinho & Xororó**: (Northeast and sertanejo · 1970) Fio de Cabelo (1982) took sertanejo, Brazil’s country music, from the interior to the big stages.
- **Marília Mendonça**: (Northeast and sertanejo · 2014) The “Queen of Heartache” put women at the centre of sertanejo. Her death in a plane crash in 2021 stopped the country.
- **Ana Castela**: (Northeast and sertanejo · 2021) The “Cowgirl”, a leader of the new agronejo generation: sertanejo with the look of big agriculture.
- **Ivete Sangalo**: (Carnival and axé · 1993) Former singer of Banda Eva and the biggest star in axé. On any sound truck, she is the queen of Salvador’s Carnival.
- **Olodum**: (Carnival and axé · 1979) The Afro bloc from Pelourinho whose drums ended up on Paul Simon’s The Obvious Child and in Michael Jackson’s They Don’t Care About Us video.
- **Daniela Mercury**: (Carnival and axé · 1991) O Canto da Cidade (1992) took axé from Bahia to the whole country and the world.
- **Sérgio Mendes**: (Pop and romantic · 1961) Mas Que Nada (1966) put Brazil on the US charts. Three Grammys and decades of success. Died in 2024.
- **Anitta**: (Funk and pop · 2010) From Honório Gurgel, in Rio, to the top of the world: with Envolver, in 2022, she became the first Brazilian at number one on Spotify’s global chart.
- **Kevin o Chris**: (Funk and pop · 2017) He popularised 150 BPM funk. The hit Ela É do Tipo swept the country in 2018 and opened the charts to the genre.
- **Ludmilla**: (Funk and pop · 2012) From funk to pagode with her Numanice project, she was the first Black Latin American artist to pass 1 billion streams on Spotify.
- **Racionais MC’s**: (Rap · 1988) Brazil’s biggest rap group. Sobrevivendo no Inferno (1997) has even been required reading for the Unicamp university entrance exam.
- **Emicida**: (Rap · 2005) A São Paulo rapper, creator of AmarElo, which became a Netflix documentary. One of the great public intellectuals of the new generation.
- **Alok**: (Electronic · 2012) Brazil’s most famous DJ, several times in DJ Mag’s global top 10. Hear Me Now (2016) travelled the planet.
- **Liniker**: (Funk and pop · 2015) The first trans Brazilian artist to win a Latin Grammy (2022). Caju (2024) was one of the albums of the year.
- **Heitor Villa-Lobos**: (Classical and choro · 1915) To many, the greatest classical composer of the Americas. His Bachianas Brasileiras joined Bach with the sound of Brazil.
- **Pixinguinha**: (Classical and choro · 1915) Flautist and bandleader, writer of Carinhoso and the father of choro as we know it.
- **Nelson Freire**: (Classical and choro · 1957) From Minas Gerais, one of the great pianists of his time. Died in 2021.
- **Noel Rosa**: (Samba · 1929) The “poet of Vila Isabel”: he died at 26 and left hundreds of sambas, including Com que Roupa?
- **Elza Soares**: (Samba · 1959) From the favela of Moça Bonita, she was named a singer of the millennium by the BBC and kept reinventing herself to the end, with The Woman at the End of the World. Died in 2022.
- **Jorge Ben Jor**: (Samba · 1963) He invented samba-rock. Mas Que Nada, País Tropical and Taj Mahal, a melody Rod Stewart famously borrowed.
- **Paulinho da Viola**: (Samba · 1965) The elegance of the Portela samba school. Foi um Rio que Passou em Minha Vida is a national classic.
- **Alcione**: (Samba · 1972) “The Brown One”, from Maranhão, one of samba’s great voices, of Não Deixe o Samba Morrer.
- **Fundo de Quintal**: (Samba · 1976) The group that created the sound of modern pagode in the 1970s, with the banjo and the hand-played repique drum.
- **Só Pra Contrariar**: (Samba · 1989) Alexandre Pires’s group, with millions of records sold in the 1990s, the high point of romantic pagode.
- **Astrud Gilberto**: (Bossa nova and MPB · 1963) The voice of The Girl from Ipanema (1964), which won the Grammy for Record of the Year and took bossa nova around the world. Died in 2023.
- **Clube da Esquina**: (Bossa nova and MPB · 1972) The movement of Milton Nascimento, Lô Borges and friends in Belo Horizonte, blending the Beatles, jazz and the music of Minas.
- **Marisa Monte**: (Bossa nova and MPB · 1987) One of the great singers of her generation, of Ainda Bem and Amor I Love You, and part of Tribalistas.
- **Seu Jorge**: (Bossa nova and MPB · 1998) Knockout Ned in City of God, he sang Bowie in Portuguese in The Life Aquatic with Steve Zissou.
- **Nara Leão**: (Bossa nova and MPB · 1963) The “muse of bossa nova”, whose Copacabana apartment was where the movement gathered.
- **Wilson Simonal**: (Pop and romantic · 1961) The great showman of the 1960s, of País Tropical and Sá Marina, before falling into obscurity.
- **Erasmo Carlos**: (Pop and romantic · 1964) The “Great Tremendous” of Jovem Guarda and Roberto Carlos’s lifelong writing partner. Died in 2022.
- **Lulu Santos**: (Pop and romantic · 1982) The man behind pop-rock hits such as Como uma Onda and Tempos Modernos.
- **Sandy & Junior**: (Pop and romantic · 1990) Siblings, children of Xororó, who ruled teen pop in the 1990s and 2000s.
- **Novos Baianos**: (Rock · 1969) Moraes Moreira, Baby and Pepeu Gomes. Acabou Chorare (1972) is often voted the greatest Brazilian album.
- **Secos & Molhados**: (Rock · 1971) Ney Matogrosso in face paint in the middle of the dictatorship, with record sales for their 1973 debut.
- **Engenheiros do Hawaii**: (Rock · 1985) Humberto Gessinger’s rock, with clever lyrics, as in Infinita Highway and Era um Garoto.
- **RPM**: (Rock · 1983) Rádio Pirata ao Vivo (1986) is one of the best-selling records in Brazilian history.
- **Angra**: (Rock · 1991) Andre Matos’s power metal, of Carry On, with a big following in Europe and Japan.
- **Chico Science & Nação Zumbi**: (Rock · 1991) They created manguebeat in Recife, combining maracatu, guitars and hip-hop. Da Lama ao Caos (1994) is a landmark.
- **Skank**: (Rock · 1991) A band from Minas Gerais who moved from ska to sophisticated pop, of Garota Nacional and Vou Deixar.
- **Mamonas Assassinas**: (Rock · 1995) With a single album (1995), they became a national craze with their humour, and died in a plane crash in 1996.
- **O Rappa**: (Rock · 1993) Rock, reggae and samba with urban stories, as in Minha Alma and Pescador de Ilusões.
- **Charlie Brown Jr.**: (Rock · 1992) Chorão and his mix of hardcore, rap and reggae from Santos, which defined the 2000s.
- **Los Hermanos**: (Rock · 1997) They moved from the hit Anna Julia to the arrangements of Ventura (2003) and still have devoted fans.
- **Pitty**: (Rock · 2003) The rocker from Bahia behind Admirável Chip Novo (2003), the biggest female voice in rock in the 2000s.
- **Alceu Valença**: (Northeast and sertanejo · 1972) From Pernambuco, a master of frevo, xote and rock, of Anunciação and La Belle de Jour.
- **Zé Ramalho**: (Northeast and sertanejo · 1977) The hoarse and mystical voice of Avôhai and Admirável Gado Novo, from the backlands of Paraíba.
- **Dominguinhos**: (Northeast and sertanejo · 1964) Heir to Luiz Gonzaga’s accordion and writer of Eu Só Quero um Xodó.
- **Tonico & Tinoco**: (Northeast and sertanejo · 1935) The “heart-of-Brazil duo”, who brought rural music to the radio for more than 50 years.
- **Zezé Di Camargo & Luciano**: (Northeast and sertanejo · 1991) É o Amor (1991) became an anthem and their story became the film Two Sons of Francisco.
- **Michel Teló**: (Northeast and sertanejo · 2008) Ai Se Eu Te Pego (2011) reached number one in dozens of countries, one of the biggest global hits ever sung in Portuguese.
- **Henrique & Juliano**: (Northeast and sertanejo · 2011) A duo from Palmas, Tocantins, among the country’s most-played acts in the streaming age.
- **João Gomes**: (Northeast and sertanejo · 2021) A young singer from Pernambuco who made piseiro explode nationwide from 2021.
- **Banda Calypso**: (Northeast and sertanejo · 1999) Joelma and Chimbinha sold millions of records independently with the brega sound of Pará.
- **É o Tchan**: (Carnival and axé · 1995) The Bahian pagode that ruled the 1990s, with choreography all of Brazil copied.
- **Claudinho & Buchecha**: (Funk and pop · 1995) The pioneers of melodic funk from São Gonçalo, of Só Love and Quero Te Encontrar.
- **Pabllo Vittar**: (Funk and pop · 2015) The world’s most followed drag queen, of K.O. and Sua Cara with Anitta and Major Lazer.
- **Iza**: (Funk and pop · 2016) From pop to R&B and samba, known for Pesadão, and a coach on The Voice Brasil.
- **Luísa Sonza**: (Funk and pop · 2017) From the far south, she became one of the country’s biggest pop stars with Escândalo Íntimo (2023).
- **Gabriel o Pensador**: (Rap · 1992) He brought rap to the radio in the 1990s, with Cachimbo da Paz and Lôrabúrra.
- **Marcelo D2 and Planet Hemp**: (Rap · 1993) Rap-rock in favour of legalising cannabis and later samba with hip-hop on À Procura da Batida Perfeita.
- **Matuê**: (Rap · 2017) The leading name in Brazilian trap. Máquina do Tempo (2020), featuring 777-666, set the record for an album debut on Spotify Brazil.
- **Natiruts**: (Reggae · 1996) Brazil’s most popular reggae band, from Brasília: Liberdade pra Dentro da Cabeça.
- **Cidade Negra**: (Reggae · 1986) A Estrada and Firmamento made Toni Garrido’s band a radio classic.
- **Vintage Culture**: (Electronic · 2012) Lukas Ruiz, a Brazilian house DJ with major success at festivals around the world.
- **Galinha Pintadinha**: (Kids · 2006) “Lottie Dottie Chicken”, the blue hen from YouTube, in Portuguese and other languages. Every parent knows it by heart.

## Film and TV

https://brazilianculture.biblioverse.org/film-and-tv.html


### Made in Brazil

- **I’m Still Here**: (Films · 2024) Walter Salles tells the story of Eunice Paiva, whose husband was taken by the dictatorship. It gave Brazil its first Oscar for International Feature, in 2025.
- **The Secret Agent**: (Films · 2025) Kleber Mendonça Filho’s thriller set in 1977 Recife, starring Wagner Moura. Best director and actor at Cannes, two Golden Globes and four Oscar nominations.
- **City of God**: (Films · 2002) Fernando Meirelles and Kátia Lund show the rise of crime in a Rio favela. Four Oscar nominations and worldwide fame.
- **Central Station**: (Films · 1998) Walter Salles and Fernanda Montenegro on a journey through the backlands. Golden Bear in Berlin and two Oscar nominations.
- **A Dog’s Will**: (Films · 2000) João Grilo and Chicó con the entire backlands and even the Devil. O Auto da Compadecida is Brazilians’ best-loved film, rated 8.6 on IMDb.
- **Elite Squad**: (Films · 2007) José Padilha, Wagner Moura and Rio’s BOPE police unit. Golden Bear in Berlin; the sequel (2010) broke box-office records.
- **The Given Word**: (Films · 1962) A man carries a cross to Salvador. It is still the only Brazilian film to win the Palme d’Or at Cannes.
- **Black God, White Devil**: (Films · 1964) Glauber Rocha and Cinema Novo: “a camera in your hand and an idea in your head”.
- **Barren Lives**: (Films · 1963) Nelson Pereira dos Santos adapts Graciliano Ramos: a family flees the drought with their dog, Baleia.
- **Pixote**: (Films · 1981) Hector Babenco follows street children in São Paulo. The young lead, Fernando Ramos da Silva, later had a tragic life.
- **Bacurau**: (Films · 2019) A village in the backlands vanishes from the map and fights off invaders. Jury Prize at Cannes, by Kleber Mendonça Filho and Juliano Dornelles.
- **The Second Mother**: (Films · 2015) Regina Casé plays a live-in maid. Anna Muylaert’s film exposes class divisions in a São Paulo home.
- **Minha Mãe é uma Peça**: (Films · 2013) Paulo Gustavo plays his own mother, Dona Hermínia. The third film (2019) is the biggest box-office hit in Brazilian cinema.
- **Isle of Flowers**: (Films · 1989) Jorge Furtado’s 13-minute short on a tomato’s path to the dump. A classic every Brazilian student sees at school.
- **The Way He Looks**: (Films · 2014) A blind teenager falls for a classmate. A delicate film by Daniel Ribeiro, awarded in Berlin.
- **Twenty Years Later**: (Documentaries · 1984) Eduardo Coutinho starts a film in 1964, the dictatorship stops it and he returns 17 years later. Cabra Marcado para Morrer is among the country’s greatest documentaries.
- **Bus 174**: (Documentaries · 2002) José Padilha reconstructs a bus hijacking in Rio, broadcast live in 2000.
- **Senna**: (Documentaries · 2010) Asif Kapadia tells Ayrton Senna’s life using only archive footage. A British co-production the country adopted. A Netflix series followed in 2024.
- **The Edge of Democracy**: (Documentaries · 2019) Petra Costa narrates Dilma’s fall and Lula’s imprisonment through her own family. Oscar-nominated and the source of political fights.
- **Monica’s Gang**: (Animation · 1959) From a newspaper strip to films, series and theme parks, it is the biggest phenomenon in Brazilian comics.
- **Boy and the World**: (Animation · 2013) Almost wordless, with a crayon look. Alê Abreu’s film was nominated for the Best Animated Feature Oscar.
- **Rio**: (Animation · 2011) An American film by Rio-born Carlos Saldanha in which a Spix’s macaw discovers his home city. He also directed Ice Age.
- **3%**: (Series · 2016) Netflix’s first Brazilian original: a dystopia in which only 3% of young people make it to the “other side”.
- **Invisible City**: (Series · 2021) Curupira, Saci and Cuca live in hiding in present-day Rio. A thriller that introduced Brazilian folklore to Netflix viewers.
- **Pantanal**: (Telenovelas · 1990) It took Manchete past Globo with nature and Juma, a woman who turned into a jaguar. The 2022 remake was also a hit.
- **Avenida Brasil**: (Telenovelas · 2012) Nina’s revenge on Carminha stopped the country for the last episode. It was sold to more than 130 countries.
- **Slave Isaura**: (Telenovelas · 1976) Brazilian television’s first major export: a hit from China to Poland and Cuba.
- **Vale Tudo**: (Telenovelas · 1988) “Who killed Odete Roitman?” gripped the nation, which also asked whether it was worth being honest. Remade in 2025.
- **Radioactive Emergency**: (Series · 2026) A miniseries on the 1987 caesium-137 accident in Goiânia. It led Netflix’s global non-English chart in 2026.

### What Brazilians watch

- **Jornal Nacional**: (Big broadcasts · 1969) The country’s most-watched news bulletin, with an opening every Brazilian recognises.
- **The nine o’clock telenovela**: (Big broadcasts · 1965) Globo’s prime-time slot sets the dinner hour and dictates haircuts, clothes and catchphrases.
- **The samba school parades**: (Big broadcasts · 1984) From the Sapucaí to the TV: two nights of costumes and themes, then a live results count that fans follow like a final.
- **Brazil’s national team matches**: (Big broadcasts · 1970) On World Cup days offices close, streets get painted green and yellow and the whole country stops.
- **Roberto Carlos’s Christmas special**: (Big broadcasts · 1974) On Globo at the end of every year since the 1970s. Without it, they say, it isn’t Christmas.
- **Big Brother Brasil**: (Reality · 2002) The country’s biggest reality show: live evictions, record public votes and breakfast conversation for all.
- **A Fazenda**: (Reality · 2009) Record’s reality show with celebrities locked on a farm, looking after animals and fighting at feeding time.
- **MasterChef Brasil**: (Reality · 2014) Ana Paula Padrão, Erick Jacquin, Paola Carosella and memes everyone repeats, such as Jacquin’s “vergonha da profission!”
- **Família Trapo**: (Sitcoms · 1967) Starring Ronald Golias and written by Jô Soares and Carlos Alberto de Nóbrega, it is considered Brazilian TV’s first sitcom.
- **Sai de Baixo**: (Sitcoms · 1996) Recorded in a theatre before an audience, with Miguel Falabella, Marisa Orth and Tom Cavalcante as a bankrupt family.
- **Os Normais**: (Sitcoms · 2001) Fernanda Torres and Luiz Fernando Guimarães are Vani and Rui, a couple with every neurosis.
- **A Grande Família**: (Sitcoms · 2001) Lineu, Nenê and Agostinho Carrara: 14 seasons in the suburbs of Rio.
- **Tapas & Beijos**: (Sitcoms · 2011) Fernanda Torres and Andréa Beltrão are friends who sell wedding dresses in Copacabana.
- **Vai que Cola**: (Sitcoms · 2013) Paulo Gustavo is Valdo, a rogue who hides out in a boarding house in the Méier neighbourhood. One of Brazilian pay TV’s biggest hits.
- **Chaves**: (Nostalgia · 1984) Yes, it’s Mexican (El Chavo del Ocho). But after four decades on SBT, many Brazilians treat it as national heritage, with a dub that became an art form.
- **Sítio do Picapau Amarelo**: (Nostalgia · 1977) Emília, Visconde, Saci and Cuca on TV: children’s gateway to Brazilian folklore.
- **Os Trapalhões**: (Nostalgia · 1977) Didi, Dedé, Mussum and Zacarias on Sundays on Globo. Mussum still inspires memes with his catchphrase “cacildis”.
- **Escolinha do Professor Raimundo**: (Nostalgia · 1990) Chico Anysio and his classroom of students who got everything wrong. “E o salário, ó!”
- **Porta dos Fundos**: (Internet · 2012) Fábio Porchat, Gregorio Duvivier and friends with their YouTube sketches, which won an International Emmy.
- **Fantástico**: (Nostalgia · 1973) The “show of life” at the end of Sunday. To many Brazilians, its theme tune is the warning that Monday has arrived.
- **Castelo Rá-Tim-Bum**: (Nostalgia · 1994) A TV Cultura children’s show with Nino, Morgana and Tíbio and Perônio. So loved that it became a record-breaking exhibition at the MIS museum.
- **TV Globinho**: (Nostalgia · 2000) Globo’s morning cartoons: Dragon Ball, Pokémon, Cardcaptor Sakura and a ritual for everyone who went to school in the afternoon.
- **Xou da Xuxa**: (Nostalgia · 1986) The spaceship, the “Paquitas” and the “little ones” marked a whole generation of Globo mornings.
- **TV Colosso**: (Nostalgia · 1993) Dog puppets run a TV station in a children’s show packed with jokes for adults.
- **Mundo da Lua**: (Nostalgia · 1991) Lucas Silva e Silva’s tape recorder and a boy’s fantasies, on TV Cultura.
- **Você Decide**: (Nostalgia · 1992) Viewers chose the ending by phone, decades before Black Mirror: Bandersnatch.
- **TV Pirata**: (Nostalgia · 1988) Sophisticated humour with Luiz Fernando Guimarães, Regina Casé and others, which changed TV comedy.
- **Hermes & Renato**: (Internet · 1999) The troupe from Petrópolis who shook up comedy on MTV Brasil before going viral online.
- **Programa do Jô**: (Talk and variety · 2000) Globo’s late-night talk show, with Jô Soares and his house band, for 16 years.
- **Roda Viva**: (Talk and variety · 1986) On TV Cultura, one guest sits at the centre of a ring of journalists: a benchmark for debate in Brazil.
- **Altas Horas**: (Talk and variety · 2000) Serginho Groisman and his young audience, with live music in the early hours of Sunday.
- **Domingão do Faustão**: (Talk and variety · 1989) For 32 years, Brazil’s Sunday afternoons, with funny home videos and Dança dos Famosos.
- **Programa do Gugu**: (Talk and variety · 2009) After decades of Domingo Legal on SBT, Gugu took his popular style to Record.
- **Caldeirão do Huck**: (Talk and variety · 2000) Lata Velha, Soletrando and Agora ou Nunca: Globo’s Saturdays with Luciano Huck.
- **Programa Silvio Santos**: (Talk and variety · 1963) The longest-running show on Brazilian TV, on air since 1963, with its famous “who wants money?”
- **Hebe**: (Talk and variety · 1966) The most famous sofa on TV moved through several networks, with a “gracinha” (“sweetie”) for everyone.
- **Cassino do Chacrinha**: (Talk and variety · 1982) A horn, dancers and amateur singers in one of Globo’s most cherished shows.
- **Jovem Guarda**: (Talk and variety · 1965) Roberto Carlos, Erasmo and Wanderléa on Record launched Brazil’s yé-yé pop.
- **The song festivals**: (Big broadcasts · 1966) In the 1960s Elis, Chico, Caetano and Gil competed live, before crowds who booed and cheered with fury.
- **Globo Rural**: (News · 1980) Country life and that opening theme on Sunday mornings, since 1980.
- **Linha Direta**: (News · 1999) Crime reconstructions that led to the arrest of fugitives, with a chilling opening.
- **Repórter Esso**: (News · 1952) “Eyewitness to history”: the country’s first big news bulletin, on TV Tupi.

Sources: [Ancine](https://www.gov.br/ancine)

## Companies and brands

https://brazilianculture.biblioverse.org/brands.html

- **Havaianas**: (Fashion · 1962) Inspired by Japanese zori sandals. They began as a working-class shoe and became a luxury item in Paris and New York.
- **Natura**: (Beauty · 1969) A cosmetics giant using Amazon ingredients. It once owned Avon, in one of the world’s largest direct-selling networks.
- **O Boticário**: (Beauty · 1977) Born in a Curitiba pharmacy, it became one of the world’s largest cosmetics franchises.
- **Embraer**: (Technology · 1969) The world’s third-largest maker of commercial aircraft. Its E-Jets fly on every continent.
- **Petrobras**: (Energy · 1953) The state oil company, a leader in ultra-deep-water drilling in the pre-salt. It grew out of the “The oil is ours” campaign.
- **Vale**: (Energy · 1942) One of the world’s largest mining companies. It is also tied to the disasters of Mariana (2015, through Samarco) and Brumadinho (2019).
- **Nubank**: (Banks · 2013) The purple card that shook the big banks: one of the world’s largest digital banks, with over 100 million customers in Latin America.
- **Itaú**: (Banks · 1945) The largest private bank in Latin America. It sponsors everything from Rock in Rio to museums.
- **Banco do Brasil**: (Banks · 1808) Founded by King João VI, it is the country’s oldest bank and among the oldest still operating in the world.
- **Mercado Livre**: (Retail · 1999) Founded in Argentina, with Brazil as its biggest market. It’s the “Amazon of Latin America”.
- **Magazine Luiza**: (Retail · 1957) From a little shop in Franca, São Paulo state, to a retail giant. Luiza Trajano is the country’s best-known businesswoman.
- **iFood**: (Technology · 2011) The delivery app on every Brazilian phone, with a huge fleet of couriers.
- **Guaraná Antarctica**: (Drinks · 1921) The soft drink Brazilians pack in their suitcases. It comes from guaraná, an Amazon fruit used by Indigenous people for centuries.
- **Brahma and AmBev**: (Drinks · 1888) From a 19th-century Rio brewery to AmBev, the basis of what became AB InBev, the world’s largest brewer, under Brazilian management.
- **JBS**: (Food · 1953) From a butcher’s in Anápolis to the world’s largest meat processor. A target of environmental criticism and at the centre of a big political scandal in 2017.
- **Sadia and Perdigão**: (Food · 1944) Cold cuts and frozen food brands that merged in 2009 to form BRF, a major global chicken exporter.
- **Globo**: (Media · 1965) One of the world’s largest media groups. For decades it set the telenovelas, the news and the national taste.
- **Melissa**: (Fashion · 1979) The plastic sandal that smells of bubble gum. It has collaborated with Vivienne Westwood and has galleries in London and New York.
- **Osklen**: (Fashion · 1989) Oskar Metsavaht’s Rio label, which dresses the world in the Brazilian beach lifestyle.
- **Tramontina**: (Home · 1911) From a forge in Carlos Barbosa, in southern Brazil, to more than 120 countries. There may well be one of its knives in your drawer.
- **Gerdau**: (Industry · 1901) One of the largest steelmakers in the Americas, founded by a German immigrant in Porto Alegre.
- **Correios**: (Services · 1663) Every Brazilian has waited on a parcel from Correios, the post office and one of the country’s oldest institutions.
- **SBT**: (Media · 1981) Silvio Santos’s network, which fought for ratings in the 1980s and 90s with Mexican telenovelas, Chaves and variety shows.
- **Record**: (Media · 1953) The country’s oldest TV station still on air. Bought by Edir Macedo in 1989, it became the second-largest network.

### Brazil and the world: brand twins

- **Chase / HSBC / Itaú**: Banks: Chase / HSBC (abroad) = Itaú (Brazil)
- **Revolut / Monzo / Nubank**: Banks: Revolut / Monzo (abroad) = Nubank (Brazil)
- **Venmo / Zelle / Pix**: Banks: Venmo / Zelle (abroad) = Pix (Brazil)
- **Experian / Serasa**: Banks: Experian (abroad) = Serasa (Brazil)

- **Walmart / Best Buy / Magalu**: Shopping: Walmart / Best Buy (abroad) = Magalu (Brazil)

- **Uber Eats / DoorDash / iFood**: Food: Uber Eats / DoorDash (abroad) = iFood (Brazil)
- **McDonald’s / Habib’s / Bob’s**: Food: McDonald’s (abroad) = Habib’s / Bob’s (Brazil)
- **Starbucks / Fran’s Café**: Food: Starbucks (abroad) = Fran’s Café (Brazil)
- **Coca-Cola / Guaraná Antarctica**: Food: Coca-Cola (abroad) = Guaraná Antarctica (Brazil)
- **Bud Light / Carling / Skol / Brahma**: Food: Bud Light / Carling (abroad) = Skol / Brahma (Brazil)
- **Kit Kat / Bis**: Food: Kit Kat (abroad) = Bis (Brazil)
- **Oreo / Passatempo**: Food: Oreo (abroad) = Passatempo (Brazil)
- **L’Occitane / The Body Shop / Natura**: Beauty and fashion: L’Occitane / The Body Shop (abroad) = Natura (Brazil)
- **Sephora / O Boticário**: Beauty and fashion: Sephora (abroad) = O Boticário (Brazil)
- **Crocs / Melissa**: Beauty and fashion: Crocs (abroad) = Melissa (Brazil)
- **H&M / Zara / Renner / C&A**: Beauty and fashion: H&M / Zara (abroad) = Renner / C&A (Brazil)
- **American / Delta / LATAM / Gol**: Transport: American / Delta (abroad) = LATAM / Gol (Brazil)
- **Southwest / Azul**: Transport: Southwest (abroad) = Azul (Brazil)
- **FedEx / USPS / Correios**: Transport: FedEx / USPS (abroad) = Correios (Brazil)
- **BBC / NBC / Globo**: Media: BBC / NBC (abroad) = Globo (Brazil)
- **Hulu / Globoplay**: Media: Hulu (abroad) = Globoplay (Brazil)

- **Marvel and DC / Monica’s Gang**: Media: Marvel and DC (abroad) = Monica’s Gang (Brazil)
