## Food

https://brazilianculture.biblioverse.org/food.html


### On the everyday plate

- **Rice and beans**: The most common pair at the table, usually with salad, a meat and farofa.
- **Breakfast**: A fresh bread roll with butter, milky coffee and fruit. The bread comes from the bakery on the corner.
- **Prato feito**: The “PF” or the per-kilo restaurant: a cheap lunch where you either pay by weight or get a full plate.
- **Bakery snacks**: A coxinha, esfiha or empada with a soft drink sorts out lunch anywhere in the country.
- **Fruit**: Bananas, mangoes, papayas and oranges are cheap all year round.
- **Sunday lunch**: The family around the table with pasta, roast chicken or churrasco.

### Dishes, snacks, sweets and drinks

- **Feijoada**: (Dishes) Black beans stewed with cuts of pork, served with rice, collard greens, farofa and orange. The classic Saturday lunch.
- **Moqueca**: (Dishes) Fish stewed in a clay pot. The Bahian version uses palm oil and coconut milk; the one from Espírito Santo uses annatto. People will argue over this.
- **Churrasco**: (Dishes) Born on the southern pampas, it became the Sunday ritual. The king of cuts is picanha, ideally with nothing but coarse salt.
- **Acarajé**: (Dishes) A black-eyed pea fritter fried in palm oil and filled with vatapá and prawns. An Afro-Brazilian sacred food sold by the baianas, who are recognised as national heritage.
- **Baião de dois**: (Dishes) Rice and beans cooked together with coalho cheese and sun-dried beef: the backlands on one plate.
- **Tacacá and real açaí**: (Dishes) Hot tucupi broth with jambu, the herb that makes your mouth tingle. In Pará, açaí is savoury and eaten with fish and manioc flour, a long way from the gym bowl.
- **Rice and beans**: (Dishes) The base of the national plate. For many people, it isn’t lunch without them.
- **Pão de queijo**: (Savoury snacks) Cheese bread from Minas Gerais, naturally gluten-free, made with manioc starch and cheese. Good with coffee at any hour.
- **Coxinha**: (Savoury snacks) Dough shaped like a chicken thigh, filled with shredded chicken and deep-fried. The queen of snack bars and birthday parties.
- **Street market pastel**: (Savoury snacks) Thin dough fried to order and served with sugarcane juice. A legacy of Japanese and Chinese immigrants in São Paulo.
- **Brigadeiro**: (Sweets) Chocolate, condensed milk and sprinkles. It appeared in the 1940s, tied to the campaign of Brigadier Eduardo Gomes, and no party goes without it.
- **Beijinho and cajuzinho**: (Sweets) The brigadeiro’s partners on the party table: one made with coconut and a clove, the other with peanuts.
- **Romeu e Julieta**: (Sweets) Guava paste with Minas cheese. The perfect match: sweet and salty on the same fork.
- **Quindim**: (Sweets) Egg yolk, sugar and coconut, a fusion of Portuguese convent sweets with ingredients from Africa and Brazil.
- **Paçoca**: (Sweets) Ground peanuts with sugar. Before it was a sweet, the Tupi word meant a mix of meat and flour.
- **Condensed milk pudding**: (Sweets) With caramel sauce, it’s the Sunday lunch dessert in homes everywhere.
- **Manioc and its flour**: (Ingredients) The staple of Indigenous peoples. It comes boiled, fried, as tapioca, starch, tucupi and farofa, which Brazilians put on almost everything.
- **Tapioca**: (Ingredients) Manioc starch cooked in a pan and filled with anything. Indigenous technology that’s now fashionable all over the country.
- **Dendê**: (Ingredients) The orange palm oil from Africa that gives Bahian cooking its colour and flavour.
- **Native fruit**: (Ingredients) Cupuaçu, jabuticaba, cashew fruit, pitanga, cajá, soursop, açaí. Many of them don’t even have an English name.
- **Cafézinho**: (Drinks) Strong, small and sweet. Brazil has been the world’s largest coffee producer for over 150 years and offering a cup is the basic gesture of hospitality.
- **Caipirinha**: (Drinks) Cachaça, lime, sugar and ice. National heritage and the world’s most famous Brazilian cocktail.
- **Cachaça**: (Drinks) A sugarcane spirit with its own protected name, thousands of brands and just as many nicknames.
- **Chimarrão**: (Drinks) Yerba mate in a gourd, with a metal straw and hot water, inherited from the Guarani. In Porto Alegre, people carry it down the street.
- **Tereré**: (Drinks) Chimarrão’s iced sibling, common in Mato Grosso do Sul.
- **Sugarcane juice**: (Drinks) Pressed to order, with lime or pineapple, the obligatory partner of a pastel.
- **Guaraná**: (Drinks) An Amazon fruit used by the Sateré-Mawé people and full of caffeine. It became a soft drink and an energy powder.
- **Vinagrete**: (Ingredients) Finely chopped tomato, onion, capsicum, vinegar and olive oil. Without it, a churrasco and farofa feel incomplete.
- **Pequi**: (Ingredients) The fruit of the Cerrado, with a very strong smell and flavour, as in rice with pequi from Goiás. Careful: it has spines inside, so you never bite it.

Sources: [Iphan: intangible heritage](https://www.gov.br/iphan)

## Inventions and science

https://brazilianculture.biblioverse.org/inventions.html

- **The hammock**: (Indigenous peoples · centuries) Europeans saw hammocks as soon as they arrived and Pero Vaz de Caminha mentions them. They’re still a fixture from the North to the Northeast.
- **Manioc flour**: (Indigenous peoples · millennia) Indigenous peoples domesticated manioc and developed ways to remove the poison from bitter varieties, a technique later taken to Africa.
- **Terra preta**: (Indigenous peoples · millennia) Dark, fertile soil created by Amazonian peoples that still intrigues scientists. The forest is also, in part, a human creation.
- **The Passarola**: (Inventions · 1709) Father Bartolomeu de Gusmão, born in Santos, flew a small hot-air balloon before the Portuguese court.
- **The typewriter**: (Inventions · 1861) Father Francisco João de Azevedo, from Paraíba, showed a typing machine before the American commercial models.
- **Voice radio**: (Inventions · 1900) Father Roberto Landell de Moura, from southern Brazil, made wireless voice transmissions and took out patents in Brazil and the US.
- **Antivenom serum**: (Science · 1901) Vital Brazil discovered that each type of snake requires a specific serum and founded the Butantan Institute, one of the world’s largest vaccine centres.
- **Sanitation and epidemic campaigns**: (Science · 1903) Oswaldo Cruz wiped out yellow fever in Rio, but compulsory smallpox vaccination sparked the Vaccine Revolt of 1904.
- **14-Bis**: (Inventions · 1906) Alberto Santos-Dumont flew in Paris in the first public take-off of an aeroplane without a catapult. For Brazilians, he, not the Wright brothers, is the father of aviation. He also popularised the wristwatch.
- **Chagas disease**: (Science · 1909) Carlos Chagas single-handedly described the parasite, the vector and the disease, a feat unique in the history of medicine.
- **The pion**: (Science · 1947) César Lattes helped detect this subatomic particle. The Nobel went only to his boss, Cecil Powell. Brazil’s national academic CV platform bears Lattes’s name.
- **Bradykinin**: (Science · 1948) Maurício Rocha e Silva discovered it using jararaca venom. Later research led to captopril, one of the most widely used blood pressure drugs.
- **The Economic Growth of Brazil**: (Science · 1959) Celso Furtado explained Brazilian underdevelopment in a classic of world economics and created the regional development agency Sudene.
- **Biological nitrogen fixation**: (Science · 1960) Johanna Döbereiner showed that bacteria can replace fertiliser on soybeans. It saves billions a year and underpins much of Brazilian agriculture’s strength.
- **The Orelhão**: (Inventions · 1971) The “Big Ear” phone booth by architect Chu Ming Silveira. Cheap, tough and easy to spot, it became part of the landscape and was exported to other countries.
- **The Stereobelt (the walkman’s grandfather)**: (Inventions · 1972) German-Brazilian Andreas Pavel created a portable cassette player in São Paulo. Years later, Sony reached a settlement over the patent.
- **Ethanol and Proálcool**: (Inventions · 1975) After the oil crisis, Brazil bet on sugarcane alcohol as fuel. That led to the flex-fuel car (2003), now most of the national fleet.
- **Farming the Cerrado**: (Science · 1973) Embrapa adapted acidic soils and crops to the Cerrado savanna, making Brazil an agricultural power, at a high environmental cost.
- **A geography of the Amazon**: (Science · 1990) Bertha Becker showed the forest is also urban and political and influenced sustainable development plans for the region.
- **The electronic ballot box**: (Inventions · 1996) General elections have been 100% electronic since 2000, with results within hours, even with 158 million voters.
- **A Fields Medal**: (Science · 2014) Artur Avila, from Rio and trained at IMPA, won the “Nobel of mathematics”, the first for Latin America.
- **Pix**: (Inventions · 2020) The Central Bank’s free instant payment system. It’s now a case study around the world: even the popcorn seller takes it.
- **Sequencing the coronavirus**: (Science · 2020) Jaqueline Goes de Jesus and Ester Sabino sequenced the virus 48 hours after the country’s first case.

## Virals and memes

https://brazilianculture.biblioverse.org/virals-and-memes.html


### Memes and legends

- **Confused Math Lady**: (Memes) Renata Sorrah as the villain Nazaré, doing sums in the telenovela Senhora do Destino (2004), became one of the world’s most used memes.
- **Ronaldinho’s crossbar**: (Memes) The 2005 advert where Ronaldinho hits the bar and the ball comes straight back, again and again. One of the first YouTube videos to reach a million views.
- **Luva de Pedreiro**: (Virals · 2022) “Receba!” and “Confia no pai”: a bricklayer’s assistant from Bahia became a global craze with videos on a dirt pitch.
- **Inês Brasil**: (Virals · 2013) Her audition video for Big Brother Brasil (“Alô, alô, graças a Deus”) turned her into an instant diva.
- **Bonner on air**: (Memes) William Bonner’s comments, “boa noites” and sign-offs on Jornal Nacional. He left the news desk in 2025 after almost 30 years.
- **Gretchen**: (Memes) The “Queen of Booty” of the 1980s became a global sticker and starred in a Katy Perry video.
- **Xaropinho**: (Memes) TV host Ratinho’s puppet rat and his “rapaaaaz”: popular humour that jumped from the studio to the internet.
- **Choque de Cultura**: (Virals · 2016) Four “van drivers” discuss cinema, with Rogerinho do Ingá and Julinho da Van. A Brazilian satire with plenty of fans.
- **Gérson’s Law**: (Legends · 1976) In a cigarette ad, football star Gérson said “I like to get an advantage in everything”. The phrase became shorthand for the worst of the jeitinho.
- **The 7–1**: (Memes · 2014) The defeat to Germany in the home World Cup semi-final became an expression for any disaster: “a real 7–1”.
- **The Varginha aliens**: (Legends · 1996) Three young women said they saw a creature in this Minas Gerais town. It became Brazil’s most famous UFO case, complete with a flying-saucer water tower.
- **Headless Mule, Saci and Curupira**: (Legends) Older than memes: the one-legged prankster boy, the forest guardian with backward feet and the fire-breathing mule.
- **The capybara**: (Virals) The world’s largest rodent is the internet’s favourite animal. In 2023, the capybara Filó and her friend Agenor Tupinambá, from Amazonas, became a national talking point.
- **Dona Hermínia**: (Memes) Paulo Gustavo as every Brazilian mother. Her lines still do the rounds in family WhatsApp groups.
- **The family WhatsApp group**: (Legends) The “good morning” with a rose and a Bible verse, the chain message, your uncle’s fake news. Almost every Brazilian is in one.
- **Felca**: (Virals · 2025) His video “Adultização”, on the exploitation of children online, passed tens of millions of views and pushed Congress to pass a protection law.
- **The Enem latecomers**: (Virals) Every November, on the day of Enem, the national university entrance exam, the gates close at 1 pm Brasília time sharp. TV cameras and crowds wait outside to film whoever arrives running a second too late, and the “latecomers show” becomes memes, with tears, desperate sprints and even people in superhero costumes pretending to be late.

### Comedians

- **Chico Anysio**: (TV and stage) He created more than 200 characters, including Professor Raimundo, and was the great reference of national humour. Died in 2012.
- **Mazzaropi**: (Film) The Jeca Tatu of hillbilly cinema, who for decades packed cinemas in the interior with films he produced himself.
- **Oscarito and Grande Otelo**: (Film) The duo of the Atlântida slapstick musicals. Grande Otelo is also a symbol of Black actors in Brazil, with Macunaíma (1969).
- **Dercy Gonçalves**: (TV and stage) Foul-mouthed, daring and free. She stayed on stage past 100, swearing at any authority.
- **Ronald Golias**: (TV and stage) Bronco in Família Trapo, with his “ô, Cride!”. One of TV’s first great comedians.
- **Renato Aragão**: (TV and stage) Didi from Os Trapalhões. With Mussum, Dedé and Zacarias he led decades of ratings and box office.
- **Tom Cavalcante**: (TV and stage) A master of impressions who shone in Sai de Baixo and created Show do Tom.
- **Tiririca**: (TV and stage) A clown who broke through with Florentina and was elected to Congress with the slogan “it can’t get any worse”.
- **Bussunda and Casseta & Planeta**: (TV and stage) Political satire in the 1990s. Bussunda did an unforgettable Ronaldo and died during the 2006 World Cup.
- **Marcelo Adnet**: (TV and internet) Discovered on MTV, he does impressions and political satire with a musician’s precision.
- **Paulo Gustavo**: (Film) Dona Hermínia, Vai que Cola and the biggest box-office hit in Brazilian film. He died of Covid-19 in 2021 and a national culture funding law bears his name.
- **Tatá Werneck**: (TV and internet) The queen of improv, host of Lady Night on Multishow, where she mocks her own guests.
- **Fábio Porchat**: (TV and internet) Co-founder of Porta dos Fundos. Now one of the country’s best-known interviewers.
- **Gregorio Duvivier**: (TV and internet) Porta dos Fundos, Greg News and poetry. One of the leading names in today’s political satire.
- **Antonio Tabet**: (TV and internet) He created the blog Kibe Loco, a landmark of 2000s internet humour, and co-founded Porta dos Fundos.
- **Dani Calabresa**: (TV and internet) From impressions on MTV to CQC and Zorra. One of TV’s most popular comedians.
- **Rafinha Bastos**: (Stand-up) One of the pioneers of Brazilian stand-up and a former CQC host, with an acid humour that regularly causes controversy.
- **Danilo Gentili**: (Stand-up) He came through CQC and hosts The Noite on SBT, with provocative humour.
- **Afonso Padilha**: (Stand-up) He talks about his humble childhood, family and real life, with millions of views on his specials.
- **Bruna Louise**: (Stand-up) She started on YouTube and released a solo stand-up special on Netflix in 2022.
- **Whindersson Nunes**: (Stand-up) From Piauí to YouTube and to packed theatres in Brazil and abroad.

## National passions

https://brazilianculture.biblioverse.org/national-passions.html


### Customs

- **The barzinho**: (At the bar) A plastic table on the pavement, a plate of snacks and friends with no plans to leave. “Just one more” (the saideira) is rarely the last.
- **Ice-cold beer**: (At the bar) Brazil is the world’s third-largest beer producer, with about 15 billion litres a year. The 600 ml bottle goes in the middle of the table and everyone shares, in small glasses so it stays freezing.
- **Caipirinha**: (At the bar) The national cocktail of cachaça and lime turns up at the beach, at barbecues and at parties. Now it also comes with strawberry, passion fruit and vodka, to purists’ dismay.
- **Rice and beans**: (At the table) Lunch on a normal day, for rich and poor. Plenty of Brazilians abroad say this is what they miss the most.
- **The churrasco**: (At the table) More a social event than a meal: someone stays at the grill for hours, the meat comes out bit by bit and everyone has an opinion on the salt. Any excuse will do.
- **Sunday lunch**: (At the table) The extended family at grandma’s, with too much food, noise and someone asking when you’re getting married.
- **Hospitality in the interior**: (At the table) In small towns and the countryside, people love having you over, and the table fills up before you’ve even sat down. Finish your plate and they’ll tell you to have some more: “you’ve hardly eaten a thing!”. Saying no rarely works.
- **Cafézinho**: (At the table) Offered at home, at the office and even at the mechanic’s. Refusing one takes some explaining.
- **Watching football**: (On screen) You often inherit your club from your family, and the choice is for life. Datafolha’s 2026 poll shows 63% have some interest in football, and 36% have none. So not quite everybody.
- **The telenovela**: (On screen) For decades, the country planned its evening around the nine o’clock novela. In 2025, the remake of Vale Tudo got the whole country asking again who killed Odete Roitman.
- **Big Brother Brasil**: (On screen) On air since 2002, it fills the start of every year with fights, memes and elimination speeches. A BBB 20 vote drew over 1.5 billion votes and entered Guinness World Records.
- **The beach**: (Out and about) Cool box, parasol, flip-flops, sellers shouting their snacks and a ball in the air. Even those who live far from the sea plan their year around it.
- **Arguing about politics online**: (Out and about) Comment sections, family groups and threads where nobody changes their mind. Many families have a rule: politics stays out of the group.
- **Arriving late**: (Out and about) A party “at 8” starts at 10, and turning up on the dot may catch your host in the shower. Work and the doctor’s are another story.
- **“Come round some time”**: (Out and about) It’s friendly, not a real invitation. Don’t expect a date. The same goes for “we must get together”.
- **The long goodbye**: (Out and about) Saying “I’m off” starts a half-hour process: one more chat in the living room, another at the door and a last one at the car window.
- **Showering a lot**: (At home) At least one a day, often two in the heat. Plenty of Brazilians are shocked to learn this isn’t the rule everywhere.
- **Gossip**: (At home) The fofoca is a national sport, played on the pavement, in the family group and on gossip pages with millions of followers.

### Sports

- **Football**: (Most followed) Top of every poll, with five World Cups. It’s also what Brazilians play most: 15.3 million people, or 39.3% of those who play a sport, according to the IBGE.
- **Volleyball**: (Most followed) The usual runner-up in popularity, thanks to decades of national team medals, indoors and on the sand.
- **Formula 1**: (Most followed) Sunday mornings with Senna’s theme tune marked a generation. Interest has been growing again, helped by Gabriel Bortoleto’s arrival on the grid in 2025.
- **MMA**: (Most followed) Anderson Silva, José Aldo and Amanda Nunes made the UFC a nationwide event, even in the early hours.
- **Basketball**: (Most followed) From Oscar Schmidt and Hortência to the NBA, which has a big and growing following in Brazil.
- **Tennis**: (Most followed) Guga’s French Open titles caused a boom in the 2000s, and João Fonseca revived the passion in the 2020s.
- **Surfing**: (Most followed) The “Brazilian Storm” of Medina, Italo and Filipe Toledo got the country up at dawn to watch competitions on the other side of the world.
- **Skateboarding**: (Most followed) Once frowned upon, it won the nation’s heart with Rayssa Leal’s Olympic medals.
- **Gymnastics**: (Most followed) A sport most people only follow at the Olympics, but Rebeca Andrade stops the country when she competes.
- **The pelada**: (Most played) The kickabout: on a dirt pitch, in the street or on a rented five-a-side court, with the same group every week and arguments included. According to the IBGE, 94.5% of those who play football are men.
- **Walking**: (Most played) The most common physical activity outside of sport, according to the IBGE: 9.5 million people, especially from the age of 60 on.
- **Futsal**: (Most played) The school sports hall classic and the training ground of many football stars.
- **The gym**: (Most played) Weights, classes and plenty of mirror selfies. Gyms are on every corner, and many people treat them as part of their social life.
- **Street running**: (Most played) A recent craze, with running clubs and packed races across the country. The classic is the São Silvestre, on 31 December in São Paulo.
- **Footvolley**: (Most played) Volleyball without using your hands, invented on the beaches of Rio. Pure showing off, and very hard.
- **Beach tennis and altinha**: (Most played) Beach tennis became a fever even far from the sea. Altinha is simpler: a circle of friends keeping the ball up in the shallow water.
- **Brazilian jiu-jitsu**: (Most played) The Gracie family adapted Japanese judo in Rio and created a martial art that’s now practised all over the world.
- **Capoeira**: (Most played) Created by enslaved Africans and their descendants, a mix of fight, dance and music. It’s practised in schools and on squares, and is Brazilian heritage.
- **Peteca**: (Most played) A shuttlecock hit with the hand, of Indigenous origin and a favourite of school breaks, particularly in Minas Gerais.

### Parties and events

- **Carnival**: (All over the country) Samba schools in Rio and São Paulo, sound trucks in Salvador, frevo in Recife and Olinda, and street blocos everywhere. Plenty of people use it to escape from it all, too.
- **Festa Junina**: (All over the country) Bonfires, checked shirts, drawn-on freckles, the quadrilha dance, corn in every form and fishing games. Schools hold their own, usually with embarrassed parents.
- **New Year at Copacabana**: (All over the country) White clothes, seven waves and fireworks. Guinness recognised Rio’s as the world’s biggest New Year party, with 2.5 million people on the sand in front of the main stage.
- **The birthday party**: (All over the country) Brigadeiro, coxinha, a themed table and the “Parabéns” song with its extra verses. Whoever gets the first slice of cake is the guest of honour.
- **Caruaru against Campina Grande**: (Northeast) The two cities both claim the world’s biggest São João: a month of forró in Pernambuco and Paraíba, a dispute as lively as the party.
- **Parintins**: (North) In the Amazon, the Garantido and Caprichoso bulls compete with giant floats at a festival in June. The city divides into red and blue.
- **Círio de Nazaré**: (North) In Belém, more than 2 million people accompany the procession in October, in one of the world’s largest religious events.
- **Bumba meu boi**: (Northeast) The story of the bull that dies and comes back to life, with costumes, drums and dance. In Maranhão, it’s the heart of the June festivities and is UNESCO heritage.
- **Lavagem do Bonfim**: (Northeast) In January, baianas wash the church steps in Salvador with scented water, in a great meeting of Catholicism and Candomblé.
- **Oktoberfest in Blumenau**: (South) Beer, lederhosen and German dance in Santa Catarina since 1984. A legacy of the immigrants, in tropical heat.
- **Natal Luz in Gramado**: (South) A Christmas of snow-free European fantasy in the Serra Gaúcha, running for months and drawing visitors from all over the country.
- **Barretos Rodeo**: (Southeast) Held since the 1950s in São Paulo state, the country’s most famous rodeo mixes bull riding and big-name sertanejo every August.
- **Rock in Rio, Lollapalooza and The Town**: (Southeast) The country’s big music festivals. Rock in Rio, born in 1985, became a global brand. Lollapalooza has filled Interlagos in São Paulo for over a decade, and The Town, from the makers of Rock in Rio, has been held in the same city since 2023.
- **Free shows on the sand**: (Southeast) Copacabana has become a world stage: city hall put Madonna’s crowd at 1.6 million in 2024 and Lady Gaga’s at 2.1 million in 2025.
- **São Paulo Pride**: (Southeast) Avenida Paulista has hosted one of the world’s largest Pride parades since 1997.
- **March for Jesus**: (Southeast) The evangelical event that fills the streets of São Paulo every year, with gospel on sound trucks. A sign of how the country’s faith has been changing.

### Cars

- **Volkswagen Beetle (Fusca)**: (Classics · 1959) The country’s best-seller for 24 years. It left production and returned in 1993 at the request of President Itamar Franco. Many are still running, and they’re loved.
- **Kombi**: (Classics · 1957) Made in Brazil until 2013. School transport, ice-cream van, mobile shop and surfers’ dream.
- **Chevrolet Opala**: (Classics · 1968) The big six-cylinder sedan was a dream car for decades, and still has devoted clubs of fans.
- **VW Brasília**: (Classics · 1973) The family car of the 1970s, immortalised in Mamonas Assassinas’ hit about a yellow Brasília.
- **Volkswagen Gol**: (Popular · 1980) The best-selling car in Brazil for 27 years in a row and the most produced in the country’s history. It left the line in 2022, with plenty of goodbyes.
- **Fiat Uno**: (Popular · 1984) The boxy, cheap “Mille” was the first car for millions. It became a meme: the one with a ladder on the roof is the fastest thing on the road.
- **Chevrolet Onix**: (Popular · 2012) It took the Gol’s crown and was the country’s best-selling car from 2015 to 2020.
- **Fiat Strada**: (Today · 1998) A small pickup is the nation’s favourite: the most registered vehicle since 2021, with about 143,000 units in 2025. It works on the farm, in commerce and on the school run.
- **Toyota Hilux**: (Today) The big pickup is a symbol of agribusiness and status, even if it never leaves the asphalt.
- **Flex fuel**: (Passions · 2003) Brazilians choose at the pump between ethanol and petrol, doing the sums in their heads. Most new cars are flex, and every driver knows the 70% rule.
- **Honda CG**: (Passions) The motorcycle that delivers everything. Bikes are the livelihood of millions, from delivery riders to moto-taxis, and the CG is the most popular of them.
- **The sound system**: (Passions) A boot full of speakers, a “paredão” at the petrol station and funk or forró at full volume. Often illegal, and always audible.
- **Lowered and customised cars**: (Passions) Tinted windows, big wheels and a suspension almost touching the road. Tuning meetings fill car parks on weekends.
- **Truck-bumper sayings**: (Passions) Truckers’ philosophy, painted on the back of the vehicle. Humour, faith and love troubles at 80 km/h.
- **Sunday car wash**: (Passions) A car is a status symbol and a member of the family: it gets washed on the street, with the doors open and music on.

### Internet and memes

- **Always online**: (Habits) According to the Digital 2026 report, Brazilians spend about 53 hours a week online, against a world average of 33. On social networks, it’s 29 hours against 18.6.
- **WhatsApp, or “zap”**: (Habits) It’s the country’s real operating system, at about 1h38 a day: for buying pizza, talking to your doctor and arguing with the family.
- **The four-minute voice note**: (Habits) Plenty of people would rather talk than type. Others listen at double speed, or reply in text out of protest.
- **“Bom dia” images**: (Habits) Roses, a sunrise, a verse and glitter, sent to the group by your aunt at 6 am.
- **Memes within hours**: (Memes) Any news story, match or awards show becomes a joke in minutes. Brazilians often laugh at tragedy, too, as a way of coping. See also Virals and memes.
- **Stickers**: (Memes) Brazilians turned WhatsApp stickers into an art form, often cut from any photo of anyone, including friends and family.
- **kkkkkk**: (Memes) How Brazilians write laughter. The more k’s, the funnier. The older “rsrs” now gives away your age.
- **Cala Boca Galvão**: (Memes · 2010) At the World Cup, Brazilians made the phrase trend worldwide on Twitter and convinced foreigners it was about saving a rare bird. It was telling TV commentator Galvão Bueno to shut up.
- **The comment invasion**: (Abroad) When a celebrity looks at Brazil, or a foreign club signs a Brazilian, the comments fill up with “come to Brazil”. Many artists have been won over, and some have been frightened.
- **Huehuehue**: (Abroad) In online games, Brazilians became famous for their laughter and a certain unruliness. “BR?” is still the opening line of any match.
- **Orkut**: (Abroad · 2004) Google’s network was a Brazilian phenomenon, with communities such as “I hate waking up early”. It closed in 2014 and people still miss it.
- **Moving to Bluesky**: (Abroad · 2024) When the Supreme Court suspended X for over a month, millions of Brazilians tried other networks and took their humour along.
- **Live streams**: (Habits) In the pandemic, the country watched concerts at home, with Marília Mendonça among the world’s record-holders. Today, Casimiro’s CazéTV shows the World Cup on YouTube.
- **The uncle’s fake news**: (Habits) Chain messages with a miracle cure, a conspiracy or a scam. A serious problem, and also a family joke. Another view: Disinformation in messaging apps has become a real issue in Brazilian elections and public health campaigns, and a subject of debate in the courts and in Congress.

### The caramelo dog

- **Who is he?**: (The dog) He isn’t a breed. The caramelo is a medium-sized mongrel with a golden-brown coat, seen in almost every street in the country. And he usually looks as if he owns the place.
- **The neighbourhood’s dog**: (The dog) He often lives at the petrol station, the corner bakery or the market, with a bowl from one neighbour and a bed from another. Nobody’s and everybody’s.
- **The R$200 note**: (Internet fame · 2020) When the new note was announced, the internet campaigned to print a caramelo on it, and the fake notes went viral. The maned wolf kept its place, but the dog won the popular vote.
- **The movie star**: (Internet fame · 2025) Netflix’s Caramelo, with Rafael Vitti and the rescued stray Amendoim, made audiences cry around the world and reached the top of the platform’s global chart.
- **Advertising mascot**: (Internet fame) Brands have adopted him to look more Brazilian. Few characters are so easily liked, across all regions and political sides.
- **The horse Caramelo**: (A national affection · 2024) During the floods in Rio Grande do Sul, a horse stranded on a rooftop in Canoas was rescued live on TV. His name? Caramelo, of course.
- **Manchinha**: (A national affection · 2018) The death of a stray dog beaten at a supermarket in Osasco caused a national outcry and strengthened calls for tougher animal-cruelty laws.
- **Adopt, don’t buy**: (A national affection) The dog’s fame has helped campaigns for mongrels. But the problem is real: animal shelters and volunteers across the country are still overflowing.

### And more

- **Faith in everything**: (Everyday life) Catholic mass, evangelical worship, Candomblé and Umbanda, and spiritism, sometimes in the same family. “Thank God” closes almost every sentence.
- **Pets as children**: (Everyday life) Dogs and cats have birthday parties, clothes and a place at the table. Owners call themselves “mum” and “dad” with no embarrassment.
- **Mum**: (Everyday life) She knows everything, says “take a coat” in 30 °C heat and will threaten you with a flip-flop. A national institution, and a meme.
- **Flip-flops**: (Everyday life) Worn at the beach, at the bakery and, for some, nearly everywhere. Havaianas took them to the world, but they were born here as the everyday shoe of ordinary people.
- **Paying in instalments**: (Money) “In how many instalments?” Fridges, trainers and even groceries get split up: 12 times with no interest is a national sport.
- **Pix**: (Money) The Central Bank’s instant payment system won over everyone from banks to the coconut seller on the beach. “Send me a Pix” has become a verb.
- **Betting**: (Money) From the animal game and Mega-Sena to sports betting apps, gambling is everywhere, and club shirts now advertise bookmakers. Another view: Online betting was regulated in 2025 after years of growth. Health professionals and consumer bodies warn of debt and addiction, especially among the poorest.
- **Beauty and looking good**: (Body) Brazil is among the world’s leaders in plastic surgery, and salons are everywhere. Hair, nails and teeth get real attention. Another view: The same pressure weighs on those who don’t fit the standard, particularly women and Black people.
- **Music on at all times**: (Everyday life) Sertanejo, funk, pagode, forró and gospel: from the neighbour’s speaker on a Sunday, whether you like it or not.

Sources: [IBGE: sport and physical activity (PNAD 2015)](https://educa.ibge.gov.br/jovens/materias-especiais/19051-pnad-esportes-2015-pratica-de-esportes-e-atividades-fisicas.html); [Datafolha via Tribuna de Jundiaí](https://tribunadejundiai.com.br/mais/esportes/interesse-do-brasil-pelo-futebol-cai-aponta-datafolha/); [Digital 2026: Brazil](https://datareportal.com/reports/digital-2026-brazil); [Fenabrave via Monitor Mercantil](https://monitormercantil.com.br/carros-mais-vendidos-em-2025-strada-lidera-onix-despenca-e-argo-surpreende/); [Guinness on Rio’s New Year, via Jovem Pan](https://jovempan.com.br/brasil/reveillon-do-rio-janeiro-e-reconhecido-como-o-maior-do-mundo-pelo-guinness-book/); [CNN Brasil: Brazilian beer](https://www.cnnbrasil.com.br/viagemegastronomia/viagem/dia-internacional-da-cerveja-brasil-tem-mais-de-1-500-cervejarias-registradas/); [Bloomberg Línea: the caramelo](https://www.bloomberglinea.com.br/estilo-de-vida/da-publicidade-a-netflix-como-o-vira-lata-caramelo-se-tornou-estrela-comercial/)

## Brazilian Dictionary

https://brazilianculture.biblioverse.org/brazilian-dictionary.html

- **Abestado**: Silly, a fool. Common in the Northeast
- **Aconchego**: Cosy warmth and comfort, as in a hug or a welcoming place
- **Arretado**: Awesome. In the Northeast it can also mean angry
- **Até logo**: See you later, even when there’s no date for the next meeting
- **Bah**: The southern interjection that does everything: surprise, agreement, outrage
- **Balada**: A party or a night out clubbing
- **Barraco**: A shack, or a loud scene in public
- **Beleza**: “All good?” or “deal”. Literally “beauty”
- **Bicho**: Literally “animal”: a way to call a mate, popular in the 60s and 70s
- **Boteco**: A simple neighbourhood bar, with tables on the pavement
- **Busão**: The bus
- **Cafuné**: Tenderly running your fingers through someone’s hair. Many say it’s untranslatable
- **Cara**: Literally “face”: a guy, or what you call anyone
- **Chique no último**: Super classy
- **Churras**: Barbecue, the basic social gathering
- **Coé**: “What’s up?”, the Rio greeting
- **Com Deus**: “With God”: an affectionate goodbye, short for “vai com Deus”, “go with God”
- **Crem deus pai**: From “Creio em Deus Pai”, “I believe in God the Father”: good grief, heaven help us
- **Cê**: “You”, shortened
- **Dar um jeito**: To work it out somehow, even if you don’t know how yet
- **De boa**: All good, no worries
- **Dá um pulo lá em casa**: “Drop by sometime.” A vague invitation. Probably no one will, and that’s fine
- **E aí**: The casual hello: “hey, what’s up?”
- **Eita**: “Whoa!” or “uh-oh!”. Surprise or worry for almost any occasion, sometimes doubled: “eita, eita!”
- **Encher linguiça**: Literally “stuffing sausage”: padding things out, talking to fill time
- **Fazer vaquinha**: “Making a little cow”: chipping in together for something
- **Feijão com arroz**: “Beans and rice”: the basics done well
- **Fio**: A thong bikini, or a shortening of “meu filho”, “my son”
- **Firmeza**: All good, solid, reliable
- **Fofoca**: Gossip, a national sport
- **Galera**: The crew, everyone
- **Gambiarra**: A clever makeshift fix that more or less works
- **Gato / Gata**: Literally “cat”: a hot guy or girl. Also an illegal power hook-up
- **Gente**: People, “we”, and an interjection: “Gente!”, “oh my!”
- **Grana**: Money
- **Jeitinho**: A friendly workaround, often bending the rules
- **Legal**: Cool, nice. Not “legal” in the English sense
- **Mano**: Bro. A hallmark of São Paulo speech
- **Massa**: Awesome, really cool
- **Meu**: Literally “my”: São Paulo’s “dude”, as in “meu, look at this”
- **Moleza**: Easy-peasy
- **Nossa**: From “Nossa Senhora” (Our Lady): “wow!”
- **Oxente**: A northeastern interjection of surprise
- **Oxi**: The short form of “oxente”: “huh?”, surprise or puzzlement
- **Pão-duro**: “Hard bread”: a cheapskate
- **Parça**: Partner, trusted mate
- **Partiu**: “Let’s go!”
- **Pelada**: An informal kickabout among friends
- **Pô**: A very Rio interjection: “come on”, “dang”
- **Puxar o saco**: To suck up to someone
- **Quebrar o galho**: “Breaking the branch”: helping out or patching things up for now
- **Rolê**: An outing, a stroll
- **Saudade**: Missing someone, somewhere or some time, with love. The language’s proudest word
- **Show de bola**: Excellent
- **Sextou**: “It’s Friday-ed”: TGIF
- **Sinistro**: Something incredible or something dangerous, depending on the tone
- **Tá ligado?**: “You know?” at the end of a sentence
- **Tamo junto**: “We’re together”: I’ve got your back. Also a way to say goodbye
- **Tchê**: How southerners address each other
- **Tipo**: The filler word “like”: “tipo assim…”
- **Trem**: Literally “train”. In Minas Gerais, it means any thing at all: “pass me that trem”
- **Tranquilo**: No worries
- **Uai**: The Minas Gerais interjection of surprise or doubt
- **Valeu**: Casual “thanks”, or “bye”
- **Véi**: From “velho”, “old man”: a casual way to call a mate, however young
- **Vixe**: “Yikes.” From “Virgem Maria”, Virgin Mary
- **Zoar**: To tease, to banter

## Records and rankings

https://brazilianculture.biblioverse.org/records.html

- **Most World Cups**: (Sport · 5 titles) The only five-time champion (1958, 1962, 1970, 1994 and 2002) and the only country to play in every edition.
- **The largest rainforest**: (Nature · 5.5m km²) About 60% of the Amazon is in Brazil. It’s the largest tropical rainforest in the world and home to around one in ten known species.
- **The largest river by volume**: (Nature · 1st) The Amazon pours more water into the ocean than the next seven rivers combined.
- **The largest tropical wetland**: (Nature · 150,000 km²) The Pantanal is the largest continuous tropical wetland on the planet, mostly in Brazil.
- **The greatest biodiversity**: (Nature · 1st) Brazil has the world’s greatest biological diversity, with around 20% of the planet’s species across six biomes.
- **Largest coffee producer**: (Economy · 1st) Since the 19th century, around a third of the world’s coffee has come from Brazil, which also leads in orange juice and soybeans.
- **Itaipu**: (Engineering · 14 GW) Shared with Paraguay, this is the hydroelectric dam with the highest total output in history and it was the world’s largest until China’s Three Gorges.
- **The largest Carnival bloc**: (Culture · 2m+) Recife’s Galo da Madrugada entered the Guinness World Records in 1995 and regularly draws over 2 million people on Carnival Saturday.
- **The biggest football crowd**: (Sport · 199,000) The estimated attendance at the 1950 World Cup defeat to Uruguay in the Maracanã, the “Maracanazo”. No World Cup match has seen so many people since.
- **The Lençóis Maranhenses**: (Nature · 1,550 km²) White dunes with rainwater lagoons, a rare phenomenon. A UNESCO World Heritage natural site since 2024.
- **The largest Japanese community**: (People · 2 million) Brazil has the largest population of Japanese descent outside Japan, ever since the ship Kasato Maru in 1908.
- **The largest destination of the slave trade**: (People · 5 million) Almost 5 million Africans were brought by force, around 40% of the whole Atlantic trade. It was the last country in the Americas to abolish slavery.
- **The world’s largest cashew tree**: (Nature · 8,500 m²) In Pirangi do Norte, Rio Grande do Norte, a mutation made the branches take root, forming a giant canopy from a single tree.
- **One of the most unequal countries**: (Economy · Top 10) No disguising it: Brazil is always among the most unequal countries in the world, with income highly concentrated at the top.
- **The largest Lebanese community**: (People · 3 to 10m) It’s often cited as the largest outside Lebanon, perhaps bigger than the population of Lebanon itself. But there’s no official count: estimates range from 3 to 10 million descendants.
- **South America’s largest economy**: (Economy · 1st) Brazil has the continent’s biggest GDP, but it isn’t the richest per person: on that measure it’s behind Guyana, Uruguay and Chile.
- **São Paulo against the world’s biggest cities**: (People · 21m) Greater São Paulo has around 21 million people and is among the world’s largest, but far from the top: according to the UN in 2025, the most populous city is Jakarta, with about 42 million, twice as many.

Sources: [INPE](https://www.gov.br/inpe); [Itaipu Binacional](https://www.itaipu.gov.br); [Slave Voyages](https://www.slavevoyages.org); [UN: World Urbanization Prospects 2025](https://www.un.org/development/desa/pd/content/launch-world-urbanization-prospects-2025)

## Fun facts

https://brazilianculture.biblioverse.org/fun-facts.html

- **Named after a tree**: Brazil comes from brazilwood, a tree with reddish wood and the first resource to be exploited. Before that, the Tupi called the land Pindorama, “land of palms”.
- **The flag is a sky**: The blue circle shows the sky over Rio on the morning of 15 November 1889, as if seen from outside the globe. Each star stands for a state. The green and yellow come from the imperial family, not from the forest and gold.
- **One of a kind on the continent**: Brazil is the only Portuguese-speaking country in the Americas and it borders almost all its neighbours, except Chile and Ecuador.
- **A difficult anthem**: The national anthem has two parts and words most people never use otherwise. Almost no one knows all of it, but sung a cappella in a stadium it gives you goosebumps.
- **The planned capital**: Brasília was built in 41 months and, seen from above, looks like a plane. Before it, the capitals were Salvador and Rio.
- **It was the capital of Portugal**: Rio was the seat of the Portuguese Empire from 1808 to 1821, after the court fled Napoleon. It’s the only case of a colony becoming the centre of a European empire.
- **Over a thousand languages**: There were probably more than a thousand Indigenous languages in 1500. According to the 2022 Census, 295 remain, and Nheengatu is still official in São Gabriel da Cachoeira, Amazonas.
- **Tupi everywhere**: Abacaxi (pineapple), jacaré (caiman), Ipanema, Itaú, Curitiba, pipoca (popcorn), carioca: thousands of Brazilian Portuguese words have Indigenous roots. Moqueca, samba, cafuné and bunda (bum) come from African languages.
- **Christmas in flip-flops**: It’s the Southern Hemisphere, so Christmas falls in high summer: Santa in a coat at 35 degrees and dinner at midnight on the 24th.
- **Cheek kisses: how many?**: One in São Paulo, two in Rio, three in Minas, and sometimes none. There’s no national rule and someone’s always left hanging.
- **Showers are sacred**: Brazilians are among the people who shower most in the world, a habit often credited to Indigenous heritage. Many shower more than once a day.
- **Time is a concept**: A party set for eight starts at ten, and turning up at eight is embarrassing. Work meetings, though, tend to be more punctual.
- **First names and nicknames**: Pelé, Ronaldinho, Xuxa, Lula: Brazilians call even presidents by their nicknames. Lula actually added his to his legal name.
- **Saudade has its own day**: Saudade Day is 30 January. And yes, many Brazilians say the word doesn’t exist in any other language, though it’s shared with the Portuguese of Portugal.
- **Compulsory voting**: Voting is compulsory from 18 to 70 and optional from 16. Results come out the same night and the country follows live.
- **It does snow**: Snow is very rare, but it does fall in southern mountain towns such as São Joaquim, Santa Catarina. It makes the national news and draws tourists.
- **The animal game**: The jogo do bicho was created in 1892 at Rio’s Vila Isabel zoo to attract visitors. It has been an illegal lottery for decades, is still everywhere and has great influence in the samba schools.
- **Pix on the sand**: Popcorn carts, iced mate sellers on the beach, Globo biscuits: the informal economy is part of the landscape, and these days you pay by Pix.
- **Carnival everywhere**: Carnival isn’t one party: Rio has parades and blocos, Salvador has sound trucks, Recife and Olinda have frevo and giant puppets. Each swears theirs is the best.
- **A mix of faiths**: It’s the world’s largest Catholic country, has a large evangelical population, and many people also attend Candomblé and Umbanda temples. Throwing flowers to the sea goddess Iemanjá on New Year’s Eve is for people of many beliefs.
- **The letter K**: Written laughter in Brazil is “kkkkk”, or even “rsrs”. A short “kk” seems cold, so people fill the screen.

Sources: [IBGE: 2022 Census](https://censo2022.ibge.gov.br)

## Wildlife and plants

https://brazilianculture.biblioverse.org/wildlife-and-plants.html

- **Jaguar**: (Mammals · Panthera onca) The largest cat in the Americas and the symbol of the Amazon and Pantanal, where tourists travel to watch it swim.
- **Capybara**: (Mammals · Hydrochoerus hydrochaeris) The world’s largest rodent, wandering calmly through urban lakes, beaches and golf courses. It always seems at peace.
- **Maned wolf**: (Mammals · Chrysocyon brachyurus) South America’s largest canid, with long legs and orange fur. It mainly eats the lobeira, or “wolf apple”, and is on the R$200 note.
- **Golden lion tamarin**: (Mammals · Leontopithecus rosalia) Found only in Rio’s Atlantic Forest. It nearly went extinct in the 1970s and became one of the world’s most successful conservation stories. It’s on the R$20 note.
- **Giant anteater**: (Mammals · Myrmecophaga tridactyla) Toothless, with a tongue up to 60 cm long, it eats thousands of ants and termites a day.
- **Pink river dolphin**: (Mammals · Inia geoffrensis) The Amazon’s river dolphin. Legend says it turns into a handsome young man in a hat who seduces girls at parties.
- **Sloth**: (Mammals · Bradypus variegatus) It climbs down about once a week to go to the toilet. You can spot them in the trees of squares in Salvador and Rio.
- **Giant armadillo**: (Mammals · Priodontes maximus) The world’s largest armadillo. Its cousin, the three-banded armadillo, was the mascot of the 2014 World Cup.
- **Amazonian manatee**: (Mammals · Trichechus inunguis) An aquatic mammal of the Amazon, threatened and protected by conservation projects.
- **Humpback whale**: (Mammals · Megaptera novaeangliae) It breeds off Abrolhos, in southern Bahia, between July and November. The population recovered after almost disappearing.
- **Hyacinth macaw**: (Birds · Anodorhynchus hyacinthinus) The world’s largest macaw, up to a metre long, with yellow eye rings and a beak that cracks palm nuts. Its stronghold is the Pantanal, and it’s the bird on our cover.
- **Toco toucan**: (Birds · Ramphastos toco) Its huge beak is light and helps it cool down. One of the country’s most famous images, from postcards to logos.
- **Spix’s macaw**: (Birds · Cyanopsitta spixii) The star of the film Rio. Extinct in the wild for years, it returned to the Bahian Caatinga in 2022 through a reintroduction programme.
- **Musician wren**: (Birds · Cyphorhinus arada) The uirapuru, an Amazon bird whose song is so beautiful that, legend says, the forest falls silent to listen.
- **Rufous-bellied thrush**: (Birds · Turdus rufiventris) The national bird, the sabiá. It’s the one in the verse “My land has palm trees, where the sabiá sings”, known to every schoolchild.
- **Harpy eagle**: (Birds · Harpia harpyja) One of the world’s largest eagles, it hunts monkeys and sloths.
- **Yacare caiman**: (Reptiles · Caiman yacare) In a single Pantanal lagoon, hundreds can be seen up close.
- **Green anaconda**: (Reptiles · Eunectes murinus) Not venomous, it’s the world’s heaviest snake, and it waits in the water to suffocate its prey.
- **Jararaca**: (Reptiles · Bothrops jararaca) An Atlantic Forest snake behind many bites in the Southeast. Its venom helped create medicines for high blood pressure.
- **Golden lancehead**: (Reptiles · Bothrops insularis) It lives only on Queimada Grande Island, off São Paulo, where the snakes are so dangerous that access is banned.
- **Hawksbill turtle**: (Reptiles · Eretmochelys imbricata) Protected since 1980 by Projeto Tamar, which turned communities that ate the eggs into turtle allies.
- **Pirarucu**: (Fish · Arapaima gigas) One of the world’s largest freshwater fish, up to 3 metres long. It breathes air and is sustainably managed in the Amazon.
- **Piranha**: (Fish · Pygocentrus nattereri) Far less dangerous than in the movies. Fishing for them is on the Pantanal tourist trail and piranha soup is famous.
- **Yellow ipê**: (Plants · Handroanthus spp.) The country’s national tree in practice, flowering leafless in winter and colouring cities and highways.
- **Brazilwood**: (Plants · Paubrasilia echinata) The tree that named the country, almost wiped out by the dye trade. Now protected, its wood makes the finest violin bows.
- **Araucaria**: (Plants · Araucaria angustifolia) The Paraná pine, tree symbol of the South, with a cup-shaped crown. Its seed, the pinhão, is a June festival treat.
- **Giant water lily**: (Plants · Victoria amazonica) The largest aquatic plant leaf, floating on Amazon rivers and able to bear the weight of a child.
- **Brazil nut tree**: (Plants · Bertholletia excelsa) It can live for centuries and reach 50 m. The harvest of the nuts supports many forest communities.
- **Rubber tree**: (Plants · Hevea brasiliensis) It built Manaus and its opera house during the rubber boom, before seeds taken to Asia ended the monopoly.
- **Orchid**: (Plants · Cattleya labiata) The national flower. Brazil has thousands of orchid species, especially in the Atlantic Forest.
- **Buriti palm**: (Plants · Mauritia flexuosa) A palm of the Cerrado wetlands, the landscape of Guimarães Rosa’s backlands. A source of oil, sweets and fibre.
- **Mandacaru**: (Plants · Cereus jamacaru) A cactus of the Caatinga. According to the song Xote das Meninas, when it flowers in the drought, rain is coming.

Sources: [ICMBio](https://www.gov.br/icmbio); [Instituto Socioambiental](https://www.socioambiental.org)

## Main cities

https://brazilianculture.biblioverse.org/cities.html

- **São Paulo**: SP, Southeast: 11,451,999 people. Nickname: Land of the Drizzle
- **Rio de Janeiro**: RJ, Southeast: 6,211,223 people. Nickname: Marvellous City
- **Brasília**: DF, Centre-West: 2,817,381 people. Nickname: Federal Capital
- **Fortaleza**: CE, Northeast: 2,428,708 people. Nickname: Land of Light
- **Salvador**: BA, Northeast: 2,417,678 people. Nickname: Black Rome
- **Belo Horizonte**: MG, Southeast: 2,315,560 people. Nickname: Capital of Bars
- **Manaus**: AM, North: 2,063,547 people. Nickname: Paris of the Tropics
- **Curitiba**: PR, South: 1,773,718 people. Nickname: Model City
- **Recife**: PE, Northeast: 1,488,920 people. Nickname: Brazilian Venice
- **Goiânia**: GO, Centre-West: 1,437,237 people. Nickname: Capital of Sertanejo
- **Porto Alegre**: RS, South: 1,332,845 people. Nickname: Capital of the Pampas
- **Belém**: PA, North: 1,303,403 people. Nickname: City of Mango Trees
- **Guarulhos**: SP, Southeast: 1,291,771 people. Nickname: None
- **Campinas**: SP, Southeast: 1,138,309 people. Nickname: Brazil’s Silicon Valley
- **São Luís**: MA, Northeast: 1,037,775 people. Nickname: Island of Love
- **Maceió**: AL, Northeast: 957,916 people. Nickname: Paradise of Waters
- **Campo Grande**: MS, Centre-West: 898,100 people. Nickname: Tanned City
