- **Nova Iguaçu**: RJ, Southeast: 785,882 people. Nickname: None
- **Natal**: RN, Northeast: 751,300 people. Nickname: City of the Sun
- **Santo André**: SP, Southeast: 748,919 people. Nickname: None

### What each city is like

- **São Paulo**: (Southeast · The powerhouse) One of the world’s biggest cities, with the country’s largest Japanese, Italian and Lebanese communities. People work hard, eat well and there’s never too little traffic.
- **Rio de Janeiro**: (Southeast · The postcard) The former capital, with Christ, Copacabana, samba and bossa nova. The inequality hits you, with favelas right beside expensive neighbourhoods.
- **Brasília**: (Centre-West · The planned one) Opened in 1960 and now World Heritage. It has the plane-shaped layout, the seat of government and few street corners: you do everything by car.
- **Salvador**: (Northeast · The first capital) Known as the Blackest city outside Africa, home of Pelourinho, Candomblé, axé and acarajé. It was Brazil’s capital until 1763.
- **Fortaleza**: (Northeast · The joker) The capital of comedy and beaches, with Beach Park and forró nights at Iracema. Several of the country’s greatest comedians came from here.
- **Recife**: (Northeast · Rivers and bridges) Frevo, maracatu, manguebeat and Galo da Madrugada. The city has a Dutch past and, next door in Olinda, giant puppets.
- **Belo Horizonte**: (Southeast · The bar city) They say it has more bars per person than any other capital. It has pão de queijo, Niemeyer’s Pampulha and a Minas way of speaking softly and doing a lot.
- **Manaus**: (North · Gateway to the Amazon) In the middle of the forest, with the Amazon Theatre and the meeting of the waters. An industrial centre thanks to its Free Trade Zone.
- **Belém**: (North · The COP30 city) At the mouth of the Amazon, it hosted the 2025 climate conference. Home of tacacá and the Círio de Nazaré, one of the world’s biggest Catholic processions.
- **Curitiba**: (South · The organised one) Famous for its express buses, parks and cold weather. It bears the marks of Polish, Italian and Ukrainian immigration.
- **Porto Alegre**: (South · The chimarrão city) Land of churrasco, the pampas and rivals Grêmio and Inter. It was badly hit by the historic floods of 2024.
- **Goiânia**: (Centre-West · Sertanejo city) A planned capital from the 1930s and the centre of agribusiness and sertanejo. The birthplace of many successful duos.

Sources: [IBGE: 2022 Census](https://censo2022.ibge.gov.br)

## Places

https://brazilianculture.biblioverse.org/places.html

- **Copacabana**: (Beaches · RJ) The “little princess of the sea”, with its wave pavement and the country’s biggest New Year’s party. Madonna and Lady Gaga drew over 1 and 2 million people to free shows here.
- **Ipanema**: (Beaches · RJ) The one from the song. It has the applauded sunset at Arpoador, numbered lifeguard posts and a summer sung in bossa nova.
- **Baía do Sancho**: (Beaches · PE) On Fernando de Noronha, reached by a staircase through a crack in the rocks. Repeatedly voted the world’s best beach by travellers.
- **Jericoacoara**: (Beaches · CE) A village with sand streets, dunes and sunset on the Big Dune. It has the Pedra Furada arch and is a kitesurfing paradise.
- **Porto de Galinhas**: (Beaches · PE) Warm natural pools among the reefs, reached by raft. One of the Northeast’s most famous destinations.
- **Praia do Rosa**: (Beaches · SC) A bay between hills where right whales arrive in winter and surfers all year long.
- **Iguaçu National Park**: (Parks · PR) Around 275 waterfalls on the border with Argentina. World Heritage, with the Devil’s Throat.
- **Lençóis Maranhenses**: (Parks · MA) White dunes with blue and green lagoons that fill between May and September. It looks like a mirage.
- **Chapada Diamantina**: (Parks · BA) Fumaça Falls, Vale do Pati and Poço Azul, with trails and little towns from the mining days.
- **Pantanal**: (Parks · MT and MS) The world’s largest tropical wetland and the best place on the planet to see a jaguar. Threatened by recent fires.
- **Meeting of the Waters**: (Landscapes · AM) At Manaus, the Negro and Solimões rivers run side by side for kilometres without mixing.
- **Serra da Capivara**: (Landscapes · PI) A park with thousands of rock paintings, one of the world’s largest such sites, defended by archaeologist Niède Guidon.
- **The Amazon**: (Landscapes · AM and PA) The largest tropical rainforest on the planet. Alter do Chão, the reserves and the rivers are entry points for visitors.
- **Christ the Redeemer**: (Monuments · RJ) Arms wide open over Guanabara Bay since 1931, at 710 m on Corcovado. One of the New Seven Wonders of the World.
- **Sugarloaf Mountain**: (Monuments · RJ) The cable car, from 1912, was one of the world’s first, and it has been in a James Bond film.
- **Pelourinho**: (Monuments · BA) Colourful mansions and baroque churches on the site where enslaved people were punished. Michael Jackson filmed here with Olodum.
- **Ouro Preto**: (Monuments · MG) The gold rush city of Aleijadinho’s baroque, with steep streets and churches. Brazil’s first UNESCO World Heritage site.
- **Basilica of Aparecida**: (Monuments · SP) The shrine of the patron saint and one of the world’s largest Catholic temples. It receives millions of pilgrims a year.
- **National Congress**: (Buildings · DF) Two towers, one concave dome and one convex: the symbol of Niemeyer’s architecture and of power.
- **Amazon Theatre**: (Buildings · AM) An 1896 opera house built with rubber money in Manaus, using materials brought from Europe.
- **MASP**: (Buildings · SP) Lina Bo Bardi’s suspended building on Avenida Paulista, with a record free span for its time and the most important art collection in South America.
- **Museum of Tomorrow**: (Buildings · RJ) By Santiago Calatrava, in Rio’s port zone, revamped for the 2016 Games.
- **Inhotim**: (Buildings · MG) A botanical park with open-air contemporary art, among the largest of its kind in the world, near Belo Horizonte.
- **Maracanã**: (Buildings · RJ) Stage of two World Cup finals, the 2016 Olympics and Rio’s derbies. A true temple of football.
- **Sambadrome**: (Buildings · RJ) Marquês de Sapucaí, designed by Niemeyer, is where the samba schools parade.
- **Rio–Niterói Bridge**: (Bridges · RJ) Over 13 km long, opened in 1974, crossing Guanabara Bay. It has one of the world’s longest straight girder spans.
- **JK Bridge**: (Bridges · DF) Three arches that seem to skip over Lake Paranoá in Brasília. It won the world’s best bridge prize in 2003.
- **Octávio Frias Bridge**: (Bridges · SP) The X-shaped cable-stayed bridge over the Pinheiros River, a postcard of business São Paulo.
- **Selarón Steps**: (Curiosities · RJ) Tiles from over 60 countries, stuck on by a Chilean artist who devoted decades to the stairway in Lapa.
- **Havan’s Statues of Liberty**: (Curiosities · Various) Outside many stores of the Havan chain stands a giant replica of the Statue of Liberty. They’ve become part of the roadside scenery.
- **Christ the Protector**: (Curiosities · RS) In Encantado, a new 43.5 m Christ taller than Rio’s.
- **The Varginha water tower**: (Curiosities · MG) The town of the aliens has a water tower shaped like a spaceship, ET and all.

Sources: [UNESCO: heritage in Brazil](https://whc.unesco.org/en/statesparties/br); [ICMBio](https://www.gov.br/icmbio)

## Historical facts

https://brazilianculture.biblioverse.org/history.html

- **The first peoples**: (First peoples · 13,000 years ago) Humans are already here, as shown at Lagoa Santa, Minas Gerais, where the skull of “Luzia” was found, and in the paintings of Serra da Capivara, Piauí.
- **A populated land**: (First peoples · Before 1500) Millions of people and over a thousand languages. In the Amazon there are traces of large settlements. Tupi, Jê and other groups occupy almost everything.
- **Cabral’s fleet**: (Colony · 1500) Pedro Álvares Cabral reaches Bahia. Pero Vaz de Caminha’s letter is considered Brazil’s “birth certificate”.
- **The captaincies**: (Colony · 1534) Portugal divides the land into strips granted to nobles. In 1549, Salvador becomes the first capital and the Jesuits arrive.
- **The African slave trade**: (Slavery · 1550) The largest slave trade in the Americas begins. It lasts over 300 years and brings almost 5 million people.
- **The Dutch in the Northeast**: (Colony · 1630) The Dutch West India Company takes Recife and Olinda for the sugar. Maurice of Nassau governs from 1637 to 1644, and the Dutch are expelled in 1654.
- **The fall of Palmares**: (Slavery · 1695) Zumbi dies, leader of the largest quilombo in history, at Serra da Barriga, Alagoas, which had held out for almost a hundred years.
- **The gold rush**: (Colony · 1695–1760) Gold in Minas Gerais brings settlement to the interior and baroque wealth, with Ouro Preto and Aleijadinho.
- **The Minas Conspiracy**: (Colony · 1789) A plot against gold taxes. Tiradentes is hanged in 1792.
- **The court flees to Rio**: (Empire · 1808) Dom João VI escapes Napoleon, brings the Portuguese court, opens the ports and creates Banco do Brasil and the Botanical Garden.
- **Independence**: (Empire · 1822) Dom Pedro I, son of the Portuguese king, breaks Brazil from Portugal on the banks of the Ipiranga and becomes emperor.
- **The reign of Dom Pedro II**: (Empire · 1840) Almost 50 years of relative stability, with coffee and immigration, while the country remains a slave society.
- **The Paraguayan War**: (Empire · 1864) South America’s largest conflict. Brazil, Argentina and Uruguay destroy Paraguay, with many Black soldiers fighting for Brazil.
- **Abolition**: (Slavery · 1888) The Golden Law frees the enslaved, with no compensation or land. Brazil was the last country in the Americas to do so.
- **The Republic**: (Republic · 1889) A military coup topples the monarchy. So begins the “Coffee with Milk Republic”, dominated by São Paulo and Minas Gerais.
- **The Japanese and other immigrants**: (Republic · 1908) The Kasato Maru brings the first Japanese. Italians, Germans, Arabs and Jews also came and changed the South and Southeast.
- **Modern Art Week**: (Culture · 1922) In São Paulo, young artists break with Europe. The Cannibalist Movement grows out of it.
- **The Vargas Era**: (Republic · 1930) Getúlio Vargas takes power, creates the labour code, Petrobras and the dictatorial Estado Novo, until 1945. He returns in 1951 and takes his own life in 1954.
- **The Maracanazo**: (Culture · 1950) The defeat to Uruguay in the home World Cup final is a national tragedy that Nelson Rodrigues called “our Hiroshima”.
- **The first title and bossa nova**: (Culture · 1958) Brazil wins the World Cup, with Pelé aged 17, and João Gilberto releases Chega de Saudade.
- **Brasília**: (Republic · 1960) JK opens the new capital on the Central Plateau, in 41 months, designed by Lúcio Costa and Niemeyer.
- **The military coup**: (Dictatorship · 1964) The military topples João Goulart. The dictatorship lasts 21 years, with censorship, torture and hundreds of dead and disappeared.
- **Diretas Já**: (Dictatorship · 1984) Millions take to the streets for direct presidential elections. The amendment is defeated, but the dictatorship ends the following year.
- **The Citizen Constitution**: (Democracy · 1988) The creation of the SUS public health system, guarantees for Indigenous and quilombola peoples, and democracy restored.
- **The Real Plan**: (Democracy · 1994) Hyperinflation ends, after reaching over 2,000% a year. 1994 also brings the fourth World Cup and the death of Senna.
- **Lula and the boom**: (Democracy · 2003) The former factory worker becomes president. The commodities boom and Bolsa Família lift millions out of poverty and Brazil leaves the UN Hunger Map.
- **World Cup, Car Wash and Olympics**: (Democracy · 2014–2016) The 7–1, the anti-corruption operation, recession, Dilma’s impeachment and the Rio Games.
- **The pandemic**: (Democracy · 2020) Brazil records over 700,000 Covid-19 deaths, one of the world’s worst totals.
- **8 January**: (Democracy · 2023) Bolsonaro supporters storm and ransack Congress, the Presidential Palace and the Supreme Court. In 2025, Bolsonaro is convicted of attempting a coup.
- **Oscar and COP30**: (Culture · 2025) I’m Still Here wins Brazil’s first International Feature Oscar and Belém hosts the UN climate conference.
- **Lula’s re-election**: (Democracy · 2026) In October, Lula beats Flávio Bolsonaro by 51.79% to 48.21% in a tight election and reaches a fourth term.

Sources: [Arquivo Nacional](https://www.gov.br/arquivonacional); [Slave Voyages](https://www.slavevoyages.org)

## Key dates

https://brazilianculture.biblioverse.org/key-dates.html

- **New Year’s**: (Holidays · 1 January) Everyone in white on the beach, jumping seven waves, eating lentils and watching the fireworks at Copacabana. Many take flowers to Iemanjá.
- **Iemanjá Day**: (Traditions · 2 February) In Salvador, thousands take gifts to the sea at Rio Vermelho to honour Candomblé’s queen of the waters.
- **Carnival**: (Festivals · February or March) The biggest (unofficial) holiday of the year. The country stops for the parades, street blocos and sound trucks. Things only get serious after Ash Wednesday. Another view: Born in Rio’s Black communities, samba was repressed by police in the early 20th century before it became a national symbol.
- **Indigenous Peoples’ Day**: (Traditions · 19 April) Formerly “Indian Day”, it was renamed in 2022 with a more respectful term. Schools teach about it and many still paint children’s faces. Another view: Indigenous leaders often reject school costumes and use the date for the Free Land Camp in Brasília, demanding land demarcation.
- **Good Friday and Easter**: (Holidays · March or April) Salt cod on Friday and giant chocolate eggs hanging in supermarkets.
- **Tiradentes Day**: (Holidays · 21 April) Marks the hanging in 1792 of Joaquim José da Silva Xavier, leader of the Minas Conspiracy. Almost a national martyr, painted with a beard and long hair.
- **Discovery of Brazil**: (Traditions · 22 April) The date Cabral’s fleet arrived in 1500. It isn’t a holiday and passes almost unnoticed. Another view: For Indigenous peoples there was no “discovery”, but an invasion. At the 500th anniversary in 2000, an Indigenous march was repressed by police in Porto Seguro.
- **Labour Day**: (Holidays · 1 May) A day of union rallies, free concerts and minimum wage announcements.
- **Abolition of Slavery**: (Traditions · 13 May) In 1888, Princess Isabel signed the Golden Law. It isn’t a national holiday. Another view: The Black movement points out that the law gave no land, schooling or compensation, and prefers to celebrate 20 November.
- **June Festivals**: (Festivals · June) Square dancing, bonfires, corn, pamonha and mulled quentão, for Saints Anthony, John and Peter. In Campina Grande and Caruaru, it’s as big as Carnival.
- **Independence Day**: (Holidays · 7 September) In 1822, on the banks of the Ipiranga, Dom Pedro I declared “Independence or death!”. Today there are military parades and, recently, political rallies.
- **Our Lady of Aparecida and Children’s Day**: (Holidays · 12 October) The patron saint’s day, with millions of pilgrims at Aparecida, São Paulo state. The same date is toy day for children.
- **Círio de Nazaré**: (Festivals · 2nd Sunday of October) In Belém, over 2 million people follow the image of Our Lady, pulling an enormous rope. Families even hold a meal like Christmas lunch.
- **All Souls’ Day**: (Holidays · 2 November) A day to take flowers to the cemetery and remember those who’ve gone.
- **Proclamation of the Republic**: (Holidays · 15 November) In 1889, Marshal Deodoro overthrew the monarchy in a military coup. People watched, the accounts say, “bewildered”.
- **Black Awareness Day**: (Holidays · 20 November) A national holiday since 2024, on the anniversary of the death of Zumbi dos Palmares in 1695. It celebrates Afro-Brazilian struggle and culture. Another view: For the Black movement it was a victory: it began in 1971, in southern Brazil, with the Palmares group, as an alternative to 13 May.
- **Christmas**: (Holidays · 25 December) Dinner is on the night of the 24th, with turkey, French toast and dried fruit, in high summer. A family Secret Santa is compulsory.

Sources: [Planalto: national holidays](https://www.planalto.gov.br)

## Politics and economy

https://brazilianculture.biblioverse.org/politics-and-economy.html


### How it works

- **A presidential republic**: (Structure) The president is both head of state and of government, directly elected for four years, with the right to one consecutive re-election.
- **Three levels of government**: (Structure) The Union, 26 states plus the Federal District and around 5,570 municipalities, all with autonomy guaranteed by the 1988 Constitution.
- **Two houses of Congress**: (Structure) The Chamber has 513 deputies, in proportion to each state’s population. The Senate has 81 senators, three per state, with eight-year terms.
- **Compulsory, electronic voting**: (Elections) Voting is compulsory from 18 to 70. There are two rounds for executive posts, with electronic ballot boxes and results the same night.
- **A very visible Supreme Court**: (Justice) The Supreme Federal Court, with 11 justices, rules on constitutional questions and tries officials, so it’s always at the centre of political disputes.
- **Coalition presidentialism**: (Politics) With dozens of parties, no president governs alone. They need alliances with the “Centrão”, a bloc that trades votes for ministries and budget amendments.
- **The Citizen Constitution**: (Rights) The 1988 charter, after the dictatorship, created the SUS, the world’s largest universal public health system, and recognised Indigenous and quilombola rights.

### The economy in numbers

- **Size of the economy**: (Wealth · US$2.65tn) The world’s 10th largest GDP in 2026, according to the IMF, which forecasts 2.2% growth for the year.
- **GDP per person**: (Wealth · US$12,000) A middle income, far from rich countries and very uneven between regions.
- **Minimum wage**: (Work · R$1,621) Monthly amount since January 2026.
- **Interest rate**: (Money · 13.75%) The Selic rate, set in September 2026, among the highest in the world.
- **People**: (People · 213m) IBGE’s estimate for 2025. With fewer births, the population is expected to begin shrinking in about 15 years.
- **Unemployment**: (Work · About 5.5%) In 2026 the rate has been close to 5.4%, among the lowest since IBGE’s series began in 2012.

### Where the money comes from

- **Agribusiness**: (Exports) Soybeans, beef, chicken, coffee, sugar, orange juice. Brazil is one of the world’s largest food exporters and agribusiness is the heart of its exports.
- **Oil**: (Exports) The pre-salt fields made Brazil one of the world’s largest oil producers, and oil is one of its main exports.
- **Iron ore**: (Exports) Carajás, in Pará, and Minas Gerais supply steel mills around the world, with China the main destination.
- **Services and tourism**: (At home) Over two-thirds of GDP comes from services. Tourism is growing but still far from its potential for a country this size.
- **Clean energy**: (At home) Hydro, wind in the Northeast, solar and ethanol. The electricity mix is among the most renewable in the world.
- **Informal work**: (Cost of living) Almost 40% of workers have no formal contract. The famous “bico”, or side hustle, keeps many families going, with no pension.
- **A complicated tax system**: (Cost of living) Many taxes, high on consumption and low on the income of the rich. The 2023 reform started a transition running until 2033.
- **Bolsa Família**: (At home) Created in 2003, it transfers income to poor families with children in school, and is a global reference in fighting hunger.

### Billionaires and tycoons

- **Eduardo Saverin**: (Technology) Facebook co-founder, born in São Paulo. He tops Forbes Brazil’s 2026 list, with around R$163 billion. He lives in Singapore.
- **Vicky Safra**: (Banks) Heir to banker Joseph Safra and the Banco Safra family, and the richest woman on the Forbes Brazil list.
- **Jorge Paulo Lemann**: (Consumer goods) A former tennis player, creator of 3G Capital and partner in AB InBev, Burger King and Heinz. A symbol of corporate “meritocracy”.
- **André Esteves**: (Banks) Owner of BTG Pactual, born to a modest family in Rio. He was briefly jailed during Operation Car Wash and later acquitted.
- **The Batista family**: (Food) Joesley and Wesley Batista of JBS. Their plea bargains in 2017 almost brought down President Temer.
- **Blairo Maggi**: (Agribusiness) From a family that became a soybean giant in Mato Grosso, he was also a state governor and Minister of Agriculture.
- **Luiza Trajano**: (Retail) She made Magazine Luiza one of the country’s largest retailers and leads the Mulheres do Brasil group. She comes up in every election.
- **Edir Macedo**: (Media and religion) Founder of the Universal Church of the Kingdom of God and owner of Record, the country’s second-largest TV network.

### The parties

- **PT**: (Largest parties · 1980) The Workers’ Party, on the left, grew out of the ABC union movement with Lula. It governed from 2003 to 2016 and returned in 2023.
- **PL**: (Largest parties · 2006) The Liberal Party, on the right, is the party of the Bolsonaro family. It elected the largest bench in the Chamber in 2026, with 121 deputies.
- **União Brasil**: (Centrão · 2022) A merger of DEM and PSL. Centre-right, with ministries and many mayors around the country.
- **PP**: (Centrão · 1995) The Progressistas, heirs to the dictatorship’s Arena party, are among the most influential parties in the Centrão.
- **Republicanos**: (Centrão · 2005) Linked to the Universal Church and with a strong evangelical base. It includes Tarcísio de Freitas, re-elected governor of São Paulo in 2026.
- **MDB**: (Centrão · 1980) Heir to the tolerated opposition under the dictatorship, it has been in power with nearly every president since democracy returned.
- **PSDB**: (Centre · 1988) The party of Fernando Henrique Cardoso and the Real Plan. It faced off against PT for 20 years and has shrunk a lot.
- **PSB**: (Centre-left · 1985) The party of Vice President Geraldo Alckmin.
- **PSOL and Rede**: (Left · 2004) Left-wing critics of PT. Rede is Marina Silva’s party, while PSOL produced Marielle Franco and Guilherme Boulos.
- **Novo**: (Right · 2011) The liberal right, in favour of a smaller state, and says it doesn’t use public money for campaigns.

### Politicians

- **Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva**: (Today) Former metalworker and founder of PT, president since 2023 and re-elected on 25 October 2026, with 51.79% of the vote, for a fourth term. He came from behind in the runoff, an unprecedented feat.
- **Geraldo Alckmin**: (Today) Vice President, former governor of São Paulo and former rival of Lula, a symbol of the broad front.
- **Flávio Bolsonaro**: (Today) Senator for Rio and son of the former president. He led the first round in 2026 and narrowly lost the runoff.
- **Tarcísio de Freitas**: (Today) Governor of São Paulo, re-elected in the first round in 2026, a former Bolsonaro minister and a central figure on the right.
- **Jair Bolsonaro**: (Recent) President from 2019 to 2022. Sentenced in 2025 by the Supreme Court to 27 years in prison for attempting a coup, and barred from running.
- **Dilma Rousseff**: (Recent) The first woman president, impeached in 2016 over budget manoeuvres, in a process her supporters call a coup.
- **Michel Temer**: (Recent) Dilma’s vice president, he took over after the impeachment and governed until 2018, with a labour reform and a spending cap.
- **Fernando Henrique Cardoso**: (Historic) A sociologist and creator of the Real Plan, which ended hyperinflation. President from 1995 to 2002.
- **Juscelino Kubitschek**: (Historic) The “bossa nova president”, from 1956 to 1961: “50 years in 5” and the building of Brasília.
- **Getúlio Vargas**: (Historic) Both dictator and elected president. He created the labour code and Petrobras and left a letter when he took his own life in 1954: “I leave life to enter history.”
- **Tancredo Neves**: (Historic) Chosen as the first civilian president after the dictatorship in 1985, he fell ill on the eve of the inauguration and died without taking office.
- **Dom Pedro II**: (Historic) The scholarly emperor who reigned for almost 50 years, until the fall of the monarchy in 1889. Admired to this day, even by republicans.
- **Marina Silva**: (Today) A rubber tapper from Acre who learned to read at 16, she was Environment Minister until 2026 and is a global reference on protecting the Amazon.

### Comparing with the world

- **PT**: Closest equivalent abroad: UK Labour / Australian Labor (Labour centre-left). Born of the unions, it defends public health and redistribution. The difference: it governs in coalitions with right-wing parties and has its base in social movements.
- **PL**: Closest equivalent abroad: US Republican Party (Conservative right). The Bolsonaro wing resembles Trumpism: social conservatism, evangelicals, guns and attacks on the courts and press. But PL itself is also a party of deal-making.
- **Centrão**: Closest equivalent abroad: No direct equivalent (Deal-making parties). With no fixed ideology, they support almost any government in exchange for posts and funding. They recall Italy’s old patronage parties, on a scale all their own.
- **PSDB**: Closest equivalent abroad: UK Liberal Democrats (Centre). A moderate centre that lost ground to polarisation. It still has familiar names but almost no votes for president.
- **Lula**: Closest equivalent abroad: Clement Attlee / Bob Hawke (The unionist in power). Union men who became leaders. Lula also stands out for returning to office after going to prison, with his conviction later annulled.
- **Jair Bolsonaro**: Closest equivalent abroad: Donald Trump (The populist right). They share a style, social media and doubts about the voting system. The key difference: Bolsonaro was convicted and imprisoned, and is barred from running.
- **Getúlio Vargas**: Closest equivalent abroad: Juan Perón (Argentina) (Father of the poor). They created labour rights through a strong state and a personality cult. Both marked their countries for decades.
- **Marina Silva**: Closest equivalent abroad: Greta Thunberg / Wangari Maathai (The voice of the climate). From the rubber groves to the ministry: a world reference on protecting the forest, with lived experience that gives her authority.

### Activists

- **Zumbi dos Palmares**: (Black rights) The last leader of Quilombo dos Palmares, the largest community of escaped slaves in the Americas. Killed in 1695, he gave 20 November its meaning.
- **Luiz Gama**: (Black rights) The son of an African woman, he was sold into slavery by his own father. He became a lawyer and freed hundreds in the courts.
- **Abdias Nascimento**: (Black rights) He created the Black Experimental Theatre in 1944, was a senator and one of the leading names of the Black movement.
- **Lélia Gonzalez**: (Black rights) An intellectual who coined the term “amefricanidade” and thought about race and gender together in Brazil ahead of her time.
- **Marielle Franco**: (Human rights) A Black councillor from the Maré favela, murdered in 2018. Those who ordered it were arrested six years later. She became a global symbol.
- **Chico Mendes**: (Environment) A rubber tapper from Acre who joined forest preservation with the right to work. His murder in 1988 had international repercussions.
- **Raoni Metuktire**: (Indigenous rights) A Kayapó leader with a lip plate, he has travelled the world, including with Sting, to protect the Amazon since the 1980s.
- **Sônia Guajajara**: (Indigenous rights) The first Minister of Indigenous Peoples (2023–2026) and one of the movement’s best-known voices.
- **Ailton Krenak**: (Indigenous rights) He painted his face black in Congress in 1987. Author of Ideas to Postpone the End of the World, he was the first Indigenous member of the Brazilian Academy of Letters.
- **Bertha Lutz**: (Women’s rights) A biologist who led the winning of women’s suffrage in 1932 and helped secure gender equality in the UN Charter.
- **Maria da Penha**: (Women’s rights) She survived two murder attempts by her husband. Her fight led to the 2006 law, a benchmark against domestic violence.
- **Dom Hélder Câmara**: (Human rights) Archbishop of Recife, he denounced the dictatorship’s torture to the world. “When I give food to the poor, they call me a saint…”
- **Betinho**: (Human rights) A sociologist with haemophilia who created Citizens’ Action against Hunger in 1993, mobilising millions of Brazilians.

Sources: [TSE: election results](https://www.tse.jus.br); [IBGE](https://www.ibge.gov.br); [Central Bank](https://www.bcb.gov.br); [Forbes Brasil](https://forbes.com.br)

## Find out more

https://brazilianculture.biblioverse.org/websites.html

- **Visit Brasil**: (Tourism · Embratur) The official site promoting Brazil to foreigners, with destinations, itineraries and experiences. <https://visitbrasil.com>
- **Ministry of Tourism**: (Tourism · Federal Government) Tourism policy, a map of the regions and official visitor data, in Portuguese. <https://www.gov.br/turismo>
- **IBGE**: (Data and maps · Brazilian Institute of Geography and Statistics) The census, population, economy and maps. The source of the country’s numbers. <https://www.ibge.gov.br>
- **Central Bank**: (Data and maps · Banco Central do Brasil) Interest rates, exchange rates, Pix and the Focus report with economic forecasts. <https://www.bcb.gov.br>
- **Instituto Socioambiental**: (First peoples · ISA) A reference on Indigenous peoples, territories and the environment, with the portal Povos Indígenas no Brasil. <https://www.socioambiental.org>
- **Funai**: (First peoples · National Foundation for Indigenous Peoples) The public body that protects Indigenous rights and lands. <https://www.gov.br/funai>
- **Museu Afro Brasil**: (History and culture · City and State of São Paulo) Over 8,000 works on African history and contribution to the country, in Ibirapuera Park. <https://www.museuafrobrasil.org.br>
- **Museum of the Portuguese Language**: (History and culture · Instituto Ação Cultural) At Luz Station in São Paulo, a journey through the language Brazilians reinvented. <https://www.museudalinguaportuguesa.org.br>
- **National Library**: (History and culture · Fundação Biblioteca Nacional) The largest library in Latin America, with a digital collection of newspapers and rare books. <https://www.bn.gov.br>
- **Iphan**: (History and culture · National Institute of Historic and Artistic Heritage) The country’s tangible and intangible heritage, from acarajé to frevo and historic towns. <https://www.gov.br/iphan>
- **Agência Brasil**: (Media · Empresa Brasil de Comunicação) The public news agency, with versions in English and Spanish, free and open to use. <https://agenciabrasil.ebc.com.br>
- **Folha de S.Paulo**: (Media · Grupo Folha) One of the country’s largest newspapers, with an English edition. <https://www.folha.uol.com.br>
- **g1**: (Media · Grupo Globo) The most-read news portal, with regional coverage in every state. <https://g1.globo.com>
- **INPE**: (Nature · National Institute for Space Research) Monitors Amazon deforestation and fires by satellite, with data followed around the world. <https://www.gov.br/inpe>
- **ICMBio**: (Nature · Chico Mendes Institute) Runs the national parks and protected areas: information for visiting and understanding each one. <https://www.gov.br/icmbio>
- **Tamar**: (Nature · Projeto Tamar) Sea turtle conservation, with visitor centres on several beaches. <https://www.tamar.org.br>

## Got ginga?

https://brazilianculture.biblioverse.org/quiz.html

- **What is the capital of Brazil?**: Answer: Brasília
- **What language is spoken in Brazil?**: Answer: Portuguese
- **Where does the name “Brazil” come from?**: Answer: A tree
- **How many World Cups has Brazil won?**: Answer: 5
- **What is the main ingredient of feijoada?**: Answer: Black beans
- **What is a caipirinha?**: Answer: A cachaça and lime cocktail
- **Who painted Abaporu?**: Answer: Tarsila do Amaral
- **Which film gave Brazil its first Oscar for International Feature?**: Answer: I’m Still Here
- **What is Pix?**: Answer: An instant payment system
- **What does “gambiarra” mean?**: Answer: A makeshift fix
- **In which city does Galo da Madrugada, the Guinness record Carnival bloc, parade?**: Answer: Recife
- **Who signed the Golden Law that abolished slavery?**: Answer: Princess Isabel
- **Which macaw is on the cover of this guide?**: Answer: Hyacinth macaw
- **What year did Brasília open?**: Answer: 1960
- **What is the world’s largest rodent, common in Brazilian parks?**: Answer: Capybara
- **Who is known as “the King” of Brazilian music?**: Answer: Roberto Carlos
- **What is chimarrão?**: Answer: Yerba mate with hot water
- **How many F1 world titles did Ayrton Senna win?**: Answer: Three
- **What is Brazil’s largest city?**: Answer: São Paulo
- **Who is Brazil’s most decorated Olympian?**: Answer: Rebeca Andrade
- **Which biome is the world’s largest tropical wetland?**: Answer: Pantanal
- **What does “cafuné” mean?**: Answer: Running fingers through someone’s hair
- **What year was the “7–1”?**: Answer: 2014
- **Who designed the buildings of Brasília?**: Answer: Oscar Niemeyer
- **Which car was Brazil’s best-seller for 27 years in a row?**: Answer: Volkswagen Gol
- **What is a caramelo?**: Answer: A dog
